summary: Research foundation for rustia: koto internals, Rust scripting landscape, Luau spec, official Luau VM, SOTA VM/JIT/WASM techniques, grabby binding+determinism contract

brief.executive_summary: rustia is a from-scratch Luau interpreter in Rust meant to drop into grabby-aliens in place of koto 0.16.1, with priorities (in order): speed, low memory, wasm32-unknown-unknown performance, full latest-Luau compat, and embedding ergonomics. The research is decisive on three points. (1) The gap is in the engine, not the boundary: grabby measured koto-int at ~5.4 us/decision (~39x the 0.14 us Rust-native floor) and koto-float (zero host calls) at 4.0 us (~29x), so ~74% of cost is the interpreted VM itself — dispatch, 24-byte tagged-union clones with atomic refcounts under arc, and per-container Arc<RwLock>. An "integer-ops fork" of an interpreter will NOT rescue hot-path perf. (2) A competent register Luau interpreter is ~4x faster than koto on a realistic interop workload (script-bench-rs "Sort Rust objects", M5 Max: mlua+Luau 11.94ms vs koto 49.21ms vs rhai 114.27ms), and the SOTA (Deegen/LuaJIT-Remake CPS tail-call interpreter) beats even LuaJIT's hand-written asm interpreter by ~31% — so matching/beating Luau-in-interpreter is the credible MVP target (~1.0-1.25 us/decision, fitting ~thousands of agents in the <=5ms-of-20ms 50Hz budget). (3) The dominant architectural fact is that the fastest native techniques INVERT on wasm: CPS tail-call dispatch is ~1.6x faster than a match-loop on native ARM64 but 1.2x-4.6x SLOWER once compiled to wasm; copy-and-patch JIT is impossible inside a wasm sandbox. rustia must therefore be a single opcode-handler core with target-split dispatch (tail-call/threaded on native, big match->br_table on wasm) and treat the interpreter as the in-browser product, with any JIT as a native-only stretch tier. The determinism contract is the gating constraint: bit-for-bit across x86_64-linux + aarch64-mac + wasm32, pinned to single cross-arch FNV-1a golden constants (AI golden 0x31c6ec2734ea6fa2; physics 9715618621526538300), insertion-ordered maps, ChaCha8/integer epsilon-greedy, a DETERMINISTIC instruction-fuel meter that must replace koto's wall-clock ExecutionTimeout, and all transcendentals through pure-Rust libm (never std, never FMA, never relaxed-SIMD). The central unresolved tensions are Luau-f64-only vs grabby's float-free i64/Q16.16 boundary, and gc-arena being the best safe GC yet hard not-Send/Sync against the "N Send+Sync VMs on a thread pool" model. NOTE: the luau-language-spec research stream returned only a placeholder ("test") — the language surface (metatables, type system, stdlib, vector/buffer/string libs, weak tables, compat edge cases) is under-researched and must get a dedicated pass before the frontend/semantics are locked. Key consumed grabby touchpoints to keep drop-in compatible live in <grabby-aliens-repo>/ (ai_bakeoff/, scenario/src/lib.rs, view/src/console.rs); the koto reference internals are under <cargo-registry>/koto_runtime-0.16.1/src/vm.rs and types/.
hard_constraints: Bit-for-bit determinism across native AND wasm32, on x86_64-linux AND aarch64-mac AND browser-wasm, validated against SINGLE shared cross-arch golden constants (FNV-1a, offset 0xcbf29ce484222325 / prime 0x100000001b3); f64 folded into hashes via to_bits with -0.0->+0.0 canonicalization. A one-OS divergence is a real defect, not a tolerance.

Deterministic monotonic INSTRUCTION-COUNT fuel meter decremented in the dispatch loop (replacing koto's non-deterministic wall-clock Instant ExecutionTimeout at koto_runtime vm.rs:674-697/3928), PLUS a separate recursion/call-depth cap at the frame-push site. koto has NEITHER; both are required must-have differentiators.

Insertion-ordered maps: pairs()/next() iterate in insertion order (IndexMap-equivalent) using a fixed seedless hash (FxHasher / FNV / hardcoded-key SipHash), NEVER RandomState/SipHash-default/std::DefaultHasher. This is a deliberate, Lua-spec-legal departure from Luau's hash-node-slot iteration order.

Send + Sync values and whole VM at VM granularity (N independent VMs across a thread pool; VMs do NOT share state intra-VM). Host closures must be plain `move` Fn + Send + Sync. Target eliminating koto's ~5-10% arc per-borrow tax rather than shipping it as a feature flag.
Steppable / yield-resumable VM (coroutine model): a scripted agent yields a ControlInput per tick; needs ExecutionState::Suspended + continue_running-style resume from day one.

serde bridge: a from_value::<T: Deserialize> deserializer compatible with serde-derive structs using #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] + default + default=fn (grabby's ScenarioSpec ports unchanged), plus a Serializer for round-trip parity.

All f64/transcendental ops route through pure-Rust libm (NEVER std sin/cos/powf); never emit f64::mul_add, never enable fast-math, never use relaxed-SIMD; restrict to the bit-identical IEEE-754 op set (+,-,*,/,sqrt,min,max). f64 is permitted only under this discipline, ideally behind a capability-gated deterministic/float-free mode.

wasm32-unknown-unknown is a tier-1 target with NO reliance on any wall-clock source (fuel is instruction-based). Browser is single-threaded twice over (no wasm threads + single-threaded Bevy). JIT is moot in-browser; the interpreter must be the always-available primary path.

Embedding API must mirror the koto surface grabby actually consumes so it is a drop-in: a Koto-like handle (with_settings/default, compile_and_run(CompileArgs::...export_top_level_ids), call_function(Value,&[Value]), value_to_string), prelude()/exports() as maps with add_fn/insert/get, native fns as Fn(&mut Ctx)->Result<Value> with ctx.args()->&[Value], runtime_error!-style errors, and a Value enum pattern-matchable in host fns.

Native integer/fixed-point arithmetic that does NOT promote to f64: integer `/`, `>>`, `//`, bitwise ops, integer `**`. koto lacks all of these (verified: `/` always promotes to f64; no shifts/bitwise/floor-div), forcing host fxmul/curve helpers — the single biggest documented ergonomic wart to eliminate.
Snapshot/restore of full script-visible per-agent VM state, cheaply enough to capture at SNAPSHOT_EVERY cadence, so MP rollback/reconcile checksums are meaningful.
Host-bridge model must support the channel/effect-queue + read-snapshot pattern (push typed effects, read an Arc<Mutex<WorldView>> snapshot) with NO unsafe World aliasing.
perf_targets: Beat koto-int 5.4 us/decision (~39x the 0.14 us native floor) on grabby's ai_bakeoff IAUS+SARSA(lambda)+contagion Q16.16 workload — source: <grabby-aliens-repo>/ai_bakeoff/README.md
Beat koto-float 4.0 us/decision (~29x native, zero host calls) — proves the target is VM dispatch+boxing, not the FFI boundary; source: ai_bakeoff measurement
Native floor reference: 0.14 us/decision = 10k agents in 1.43ms (aarch64 Mac, release opt-level 3) — the asymptotic prize

AI time budget: <=5 ms of a 20 ms (50 Hz) tick, single-threaded, on the SLOWEST target (web/iOS); threads are a bonus, never load-bearing. koto-int caps at ~900 agents, koto-float ~1250; native does 10k

MVP target: match Luau-in-interpreter (~4.1x faster than koto on script-bench-rs: mlua+Luau 11.94ms vs koto 49.21ms; mlua Lua5.5 15.72ms; rhai 114.27ms tree-walker) -> would cut grabby to ~1.0-1.25 us/decision
Stretch target: ~10x koto-int -> ~0.54 us/decision (~4x native) -> 10k agents ~5.4ms -> scripted per-tick-per-agent hot path viable to ~9000 agents single-threaded
SOTA interpreter ceiling: Deegen/LJR CPS tail-call interpreter is +31% over LuaJIT's asm interpreter and +179% over PUC-Lua across 44 benchmarks (arXiv 2411.11469)
SOTA native baseline-JIT ceiling: copy-and-patch within ~34% of full LuaJIT, 4.6x PUC-Lua, codegen 1.62 GB/s, ~91 bytes/bytecode, <1ms for 17,197 bytecodes — NATIVE ONLY
Keep interpreter core+builtins small (Luau is ~16 KB on x64, fits L1i) for sustained dispatch throughput
wasm in-browser tax is an OPEN GATE: feared ~4x, optimistic 1.5-2.5x — requires a MEASURED real-browser number, not extrapolation (the gate koto never cleared)
Eliminate koto's ~5-10% arc per-borrow tax (atomic refcount + parking_lot RwLock per container access) by using non-atomic Rc-inside-VM + Send-at-VM-granularity

Re-bench identically behind grabby's Selector trait using its Criterion harness (harness=false, opt-level 3, n in {1000,2000,5000,10000}, b.iter(|| world.tick_with(sel); black_box(world.state_hash())))

reusable_components.use_for: Safe incremental cycle-detecting non-moving mark&sweep GC with word-sized Copy Gc<'gc,T> pointers, memory-tracked for fuel; its mutate-XOR-collect invariant naturally forces the exact stackless/steppable VM rustia needs
reusable_components.recommendation: Best safe-GC design AND fuel-friendly, production-proven (Ruffle) — BUT Arena/Gc are hard NOT Send and NOT Sync, colliding with N-Send+Sync-VMs. Adopt the IDEA; either keep VMs strictly thread-local (move work not VMs), fork for Send-but-not-Sync per-VM migration, or reject tracing GC for RC. Read 0.5.x source for the exact auto-trait/'gc-brand situation before betting on it.

reusable_components.use_for: Stackless/trampoline register-VM architecture: reified call stack polled via Executor::step(fuel), callbacks as Sequence multi-step objects -> deterministic fuel + recursion limit + DoS resilience essentially for free
reusable_components.recommendation: Study/port the architecture, do NOT fork wholesale for perf: pre-1.0, author states the interp loop is unoptimized and not competitive with LuaJIT/Luau, it's Lua 5.x not Luau, and it inherits the gc-arena Send blocker. Ergonomic cost: native callbacks that re-enter the VM must be poll-style Sequences.

reusable_components.use_for: Lossless multi-dialect parser INCLUDING Luau (LuaVersion flag), error recovery via AstResult; battle-tested as the StyLua/selene frontend
reusable_components.recommendation: Use as Luau-compat correctness oracle and bootstrap frontend; its trivia-rich lossless AST is built for tooling and is too heavy/slow to feed a bytecode compiler directly — budget a trivia-stripping lowering pass or an eventual purpose-built lexer+parser. Benchmark against luau-parser (claims 'blazingly fast') before committing.

reusable_components.use_for: Embedding-API ergonomics gold standard: UserData (add_method/add_meta_method/add_field), FromLua/IntoLua (+multi-value), Scope for non-'static borrows, UserDataRef/Mut guards, blanket impls over Rc/Arc wrappers, async-over-coroutines
reusable_components.recommendation: Mirror the surface (adjusted so handles are Send under the arc-equivalent build); reference only, do NOT depend — it is C bindings to PUC/LuaJIT/Luau, not pure Rust, so unusable as a wasm-clean engine.

reusable_components.use_for: Determinism map model (IndexMap<ValueKey,KValue,FxHasher>, types/map.rs) to copy verbatim; Rc<->Arc compile-time feature-swap Send model (koto_memory/lib.rs); dual KNumber{I64,F64} number template (types/number.rs); the exact embedding API contract grabby depends on (koto-0.16.1/src/koto.rs)
reusable_components.recommendation: Copy the insertion-ordered seedless-hash map and the Send-via-feature-swap idea; keep a dual-number internal representation; pin the consumed API as a compatibility shim. Avoid its weaknesses: two-level dispatch (169-variant Instruction enum built by value per step), always-heap strings (no SSO), per-call register Vec Null-fill, Arc<RwLock> per container, no fuel, no recursion cap, cycle leaks.

reusable_components.use_for: Deterministic cross-arch transcendentals (sin/cos/exp/pow/log/fmod) and LUT construction
reusable_components.recommendation: Mandatory for any f64 surface and for Q16.16 LUT building (the rapier-proven cross-platform-determinism recipe; already grabby's rule). Typically slower than system libm — measure, but correctness is non-negotiable. Core +,-,*,/,sqrt on f64 are already bit-deterministic and need no special handling.

reusable_components.use_for: Reference for the register VM + 32-bit fixed-width instruction encoding (Bytecode.h), self-patching inline caches (GETTABLEKS, lvmexecute.cpp:512-542), load-time GETIMPORT, FASTCALL path (133 LBF_ builtins, no call frame), hybrid array+hash tables, incremental non-moving mark&sweep with allocation-driven pacing (lgc.cpp), and the NEW int64 LUA_TINTEGER subtype (lua.h:77, lapi.cpp)
reusable_components.recommendation: Port techniques not code. Adopt register VM + AUX-word encoding (highest-ROI structural decision), inline caches (determinism-safe: affect only speed), GETIMPORT/FASTCALL, and the int64 subtype to resolve the f64 tension — but note int64 is gated behind FFlags and NOT yet folded into the hot arith opcodes in Luau itself, so its arithmetic reach needs verification.

reusable_components.use_for: Native-only tier-1 baseline JIT (copy-and-patch: 1.62 GB/s codegen, within ~34% of LuaJIT)
reusable_components.recommendation: Native-only, gated cfg(not(target_arch="wasm32")), and a STRETCH not MVP. A Rust copy-and-patch stencil pipeline is non-trivial (Deegen relies on clang asm-goto/CallBr + LLVM build-time tooling); prefer cranelift for maintainability if stencil tooling proves too costly. Never attempt runtime wasm-module emission for hotpaths.

reusable_components.use_for: grabby's established deterministic RNG (per-entity substreams seed=FNV-1a(entity_id,tick), count-independent) and state hashing; integer epsilon-greedy ((rng.next_u32()&1023)<51)
reusable_components.recommendation: Keep verbatim and portable; expose rand()/rand_range() to script via host-side integer math. Never use StdRng/thread_rng/DefaultHasher.
Use as-is (or a custom insertion-ordered open-addressing map for memory/speed); guarantees free bit-for-bit map ordering. Never expose a randomized hasher.

design_axes.why_it_matters: ~74% of grabby's cost is the interpreter VM, and dispatch is the single highest-ROI lever — but the fastest native technique INVERTS on wasm (CPS tail-call is ~1.6x faster than match-loop on native ARM64, yet 1.2x-4.6x SLOWER compiled to wasm; computed-goto cannot exist in wasm). koto compounds this with two-level dispatch (decode into a 169-variant enum by value, then match).
candidate_directions: Target-split single-source dispatch (RECOMMENDED baseline): one set of opcode handlers; CPS tail-call / context-threaded on native via nightly `become`+extern "rust-preserve-none" (Deegen-class, targets +31% over LuaJIT interp), big match->br_table switch-loop under cfg(target_arch="wasm32").
Single portable loop+match everywhere that the compiler lowers to a jump table — simplest, accepts leaving native perf on the table; safe stable-Rust fallback.

Closure/threaded-code: compile bytecode to a tree of boxed Rust closures (or fn-pointer chain) at load time, eliminating per-op decode and enum-build, fuel threaded through closures — works on wasm, middle ground between interpret and JIT.
Fused decode+execute over fixed-width encoding read in-loop (kill koto's per-step 169-variant Instruction enum) with no threading — low-risk incremental win over koto.
Two-tier: portable interpreter everywhere + copy-and-patch or cranelift baseline JIT gated cfg(not(wasm32)); fuel decrements injected into generated stencils to preserve determinism.

design_axes.why_it_matters: koto's 24-byte cloned tagged union with atomic refcounts dominates its hot path (clone_register on every Copy/Call/Return); memory is priority #2; and wasm's 32-bit pointers flip the NaN-boxing tradeoff (an 8-byte value can carry a double OR a 32-bit GC handle+tag, halving value memory and roughly doubling cache density).
candidate_directions: 16-byte Luau-faithful tagged union (8B payload union + 4B extra + 4B tag), inline 3xf32 vector as a first-class type, branch-friendly — best native, Luau-compatible, simplest port (Luau deliberately rejects NaN-boxing).
8-byte NaN-boxed value tuned for wasm32 32-bit handles — halves memory/linear-memory traffic, but the native 3xf32 vector must be boxed and it REQUIRES NaN canonicalization for determinism.
koto-style 24-byte enum with niche-packing + dual KNumber{I64,F64} — proven, simplest in safe Rust, but heaviest and forces refcount churn.
Tagged value + small-string-optimization (SSO) inline + interned identifiers/map keys — directly attacks koto's always-heap strings (low-hanging speed+memory).
Per-target hybrid (cfg): NaN-box on wasm32, 16-byte tagged on native — benchmark both before committing (priorities put speed #1, memory #2; mask/shift cost vs 2x memory traffic is empirical).

design_axes.axis: Number model / determinism strategy (f64 vs fixed-point)
design_axes.why_it_matters: Luau is f64-only (no integer subtype in the language spec) while grabby's hard determinism boundary passes only i64/Q16.16 with all f64 math in Rust — the central semantic tension. Determinism is priority #1; full Luau compat is priority #4.
candidate_directions: f64-internal + mandatory pure-Rust libm + no-FMA/no-fast-math/no-relaxed-SIMD discipline, pinned by single cross-arch golden (RECOMMENDED default): keeps full Luau f64 compat with bit-identical native/wasm results.

First-class int64 subtype (mirroring Luau 727 LUA_TINTEGER) + Q16.16 intrinsics providing integer `/`,`>>`,`//`,bitwise,`**` — resolves the host-helper wart and stays Luau-727-aligned (verify how far integer support reaches into arith opcodes).

Strict float-free mode: capability-gate every f64-touching op (float<->string, fmod/%, float compare/sort, map-key hashing, **, int<->float coercion) out of the prelude — zero-risk determinism, deliberately non-conformant Luau.
koto dual-number KNumber{I64,F64} verbatim — proven and determinism-equivalent in grabby's koto-int path, but is a Luau-semantics divergence that must define exactly when a value is I64 vs F64.
Build-mode fork: ship BOTH an f64-deterministic mode and a fixed-point/Q16.16 mode selectable at build time, plus a fuel/LOD knob so leaf cadence is tunable.

design_axes.why_it_matters: koto reference-counts with NO cycle detection (cycles leak) and pays an Arc<parking_lot::RwLock> tax per container access under arc; rustia needs Send+Sync at VM granularity, low memory, deterministic collection timing, and fuel-driven pacing — and the best safe GC (gc-arena) is hard not-Send/Sync.
candidate_directions: Reference counting with non-atomic Rc-inside-VM + Send-at-VM-granularity (move the whole VM across pool threads, never share intra-VM state) — eliminates atomic refcounts AND RwLock locks; the single biggest structural win over koto-arc; accepts cycle leaks like koto.
koto's Rc<->Arc compile-time feature swap — proven Send, but keeps the ~5-10% per-borrow tax and the cycle leak.

gc-arena incremental non-moving cycle-collecting mark&sweep, one Arena per VM, GC stepped off the same deterministic fuel counter — best safety+memory, but must solve the Send blocker (thread-local VMs or a fork).

Hand-rolled incremental NON-moving NON-generational mark&sweep (Luau-style, allocation/fuel-driven pacing; non-moving keeps inline-cache pointers/handles stable), engineered Send-but-not-Sync per VM (gluon-style separate heap per VM).
RC now + optional trial-deletion cycle collector added later, with a per-VM heap reset between episodes as a pragmatic leak bound for long-running thousands-of-agents sims.

design_axes.why_it_matters: Priority #3 is wasm performance and JIT is moot in-browser; copy-and-patch needs to write executable native bytes (impossible in the wasm sandbox), and runtime wasm-module emission (Wingo) loses to a good interpreter for short per-agent scripts (instantiate cost + sync-compile size caps + call_indirect indirection). The interpreter IS the in-browser product.
candidate_directions: Interpreter-only on wasm (RECOMMENDED): make it excellent — maximize dispatch quality and minimize dispatch COUNT via fat superinstructions (Luau FORGLOOP/NAMECALL/FASTCALL/GETIMPORT) and inline caches that degrade to a guarded branch + side table on wasm; native gets the JIT tier.
Native copy-and-patch baseline JIT (1.62 GB/s, ~34% off LuaJIT) gated cfg(not(wasm32)) — fastest native tier, complex Rust stencil pipeline.
Native cranelift baseline JIT — maintainability over compile speed, easier Rust integration than copy-and-patch.
AOT-compile fully-typed hot kernels (not general scripts) to wasm modules for near-native in-browser speed — niche; loses deterministic fuel/stepping for those kernels; low priority.
Reject runtime in-wasm code generation (Wingo path) for hotpaths and document it as non-viable — preserves engineering focus on the interpreter.

design_axes.why_it_matters: Full latest-Luau compat is priority #4 and parser correctness is the hardest part to get right for compat; compile/hot-reload latency is an explicit DX deciding factor (koto's instant re-eval is a cited win). CRITICAL: the dedicated luau-language-spec research stream came back empty (placeholder 'test'), so the language surface is under-researched.
candidate_directions: full_moon frontend + trivia-stripping lowering -> rustia's own register-bytecode compiler (de-risks Luau-syntax compat, reuses a battle-tested parser).
Custom hand-written Luau lexer+parser optimized to feed the bytecode compiler directly — full control and best compile speed, highest effort and compat risk.
luau-parser crate ('blazingly fast') as the runtime frontend, full_moon as the offline correctness oracle — dual track.
Transliterate Luau's own C++ compiler passes (constant folding, FASTCALL recognition, inlining, loop unrolling) to Rust but emit rustia's deterministic bytecode — highest fidelity, highest effort.

Commission a dedicated Luau-language-spec research pass FIRST (metatables, type system, stdlib, vector/buffer/string libs, weak tables/__gc, compat edge cases) before locking any frontend — the missing stream is a prerequisite, not optional.

design_axes.why_it_matters: Priority #5 and the literal drop-in requirement: rustia must replace koto behind grabby's existing call sites and Selector trait, and DX (REPL, hot-reload latency, LSP) is a deciding factor gak cares about. Per-call KValue marshalling is real overhead at thousands of agents.
candidate_directions: koto-compatible shim API matching the exact consumed surface (with_settings, prelude().add_fn/insert, exports().get, compile_and_run(export_top_level_ids), call_function, value_to_string, is_callable) — guarantees drop-in.
mlua-style idiomatic API (UserData, FromLua/IntoLua, Scope, UserDataRef guards) — richer, more ergonomic, more work.
Both: a koto-compat facade layered over an mlua-style core, so grabby ports unchanged while new code uses the nicer API.
Batched/vectorized host entry ('decide N agents in one VM call') to amortize per-call marshalling — lets a slower-per-call VM still hit the aggregate <=5ms budget.
First-class channel/effect-queue host-bridge (push typed effects, read an Arc<Mutex<WorldView>> snapshot; no unsafe World aliasing), host fns get a typed arg slice and return Value or runtime error.

design_axes.why_it_matters: Replacing koto's wall-clock limit with bit-deterministic instruction-fuel + a recursion cap is a hard constraint; the VM must yield per-tick ControlInput; and MP rollback needs cheap exact snapshot/restore of script-visible state — all of which interact with the dispatch design and any JIT tier.
candidate_directions: Stackless trampoline executor (piccolo-style): reified call stack, step(fuel), native callbacks as poll-style Sequences — DoS-resilient and fuel-native, at an ergonomic cost.

Native-stack interpreter with explicit fuel decrement in the dispatch loop + an explicit call-depth cap at frame-push (recursion bounded by a reified call_stack Vec, not the native stack) — simpler, straight-line callbacks.
Inject fuel decrements into JIT-generated stencils so tiering up preserves identical instruction-count semantics across interpreter and native JIT.
Yield-resumable coroutine model (ExecutionState::Suspended + continue_running) as the per-tick agent interface, with fuel budget per resume.

Snapshot/restore strategy fork: full flat VM-state serialization (registers + reified call stack + heap) every SNAPSHOT_EVERY vs delta/coarse-cadence capture — design value layout to be cheaply serializable up front.

key_tensions: Luau is f64-only (no language-level integer subtype) vs grabby's float-free i64/Q16.16 determinism boundary. Resolutions are mutually exclusive in flavor: f64-internal+libm+no-FMA (most Luau-compatible), a first-class int64 subtype a la Luau-727 LUA_TINTEGER (note: not yet wired into Luau's hot arith opcodes), or a strict float-free mode (zero-risk determinism, non-conformant).

gc-arena is the best safe, incremental, cycle-collecting, fuel-trackable GC AND its mutate-XOR-collect invariant forces exactly the stackless steppable VM rustia wants — but it is fundamentally NOT Send and NOT Sync, directly colliding with 'N independent Send+Sync VMs across a thread pool.' Either thread-local VMs (move work not VMs), a Send-but-not-Sync fork, or reject tracing GC for reference counting.

JIT is the real performance prize (copy-and-patch within ~34% of LuaJIT native) but is moot in-browser, and copy-and-patch literally cannot run inside a wasm sandbox. Forces a dual engine: interpreter-primary (the wasm product) + optional native-only JIT tier.

The fastest native dispatch (CPS tail-call/computed-goto-equivalent, ~1.6x over match-loop, +31% over LuaJIT's asm interpreter) INVERTS on wasm, regressing 1.2x-4.6x. Dispatch must be a per-target strategy (tail-call/threaded native, big match->br_table on wasm), not one universal design.

8-byte NaN-boxing (serves low-memory priority #2 and wasm linear-memory cache pressure, mask/shift per access) vs 16-byte tagged value (faster, branch-friendlier, enables a native 3xf32 vector type, Luau-faithful). The right answer is empirical and may differ native vs wasm.

Insertion-ordered maps (determinism hard constraint) vs Luau's actual hash-node-slot iteration order. The divergence is Lua-spec-legal but is a deliberate departure from Luau table internals and interacts awkwardly with inline-cache hidden-class shapes (shape explosion / shape-id determinism on key delete/re-add).

Full latest-Luau compat (priority #4) vs a custom deterministic bytecode/value model: high-fidelity compat (metatables, vector type, buffer lib, weak tables, __gc) may force tracking Luau VM semantics so closely that reusing Luau's own compiler becomes cheaper — while weak tables + __gc finalizer order are themselves determinism hazards.

Closing grabby's ~29-39x gap demands deep VM work (better dispatch + value layout + GC + possibly JIT); an interpreter that merely adds integer ops will NOT close it (koto-float is still 4.0us with zero host calls). Yet on wasm the JIT lever is unavailable, capping the in-browser ceiling at interpreter quality.
RC cycle leaks (koto tolerates them) vs long-running sims with thousands of agents holding per-agent Q-tables/traces — may mandate a cycle collector, which re-raises the gc-arena Send problem.
Deterministic f64 via pure-Rust libm is achievable but libm is typically slower than system libm — a determinism-vs-speed micro-tension on every transcendental.

Stackless trampoline executor (fuel-native, DoS-safe, snapshot-friendly) vs straight-line ergonomic native callbacks — the safe design forces poll-style Sequence callbacks, raising embedding-API complexity.

risk_register.risk: gc-arena (the most attractive GC) is hard NOT Send/Sync, conflicting with the N-Send+Sync-VMs constraint; choosing it could block the threading model late.
risk_register.mitigation: Default to reference counting with Rc-inside-VM + Send-at-VM-granularity (move whole VMs). If a cycle collector proves necessary, prototype a Send-but-not-Sync fork or a hand-rolled non-moving mark&sweep per VM EARLY and prove VM migration between pool threads before committing.

risk_register.risk: wasm in-browser interpreter tax is unknown and feared up to ~4x — the gate koto never cleared; the whole priority-#3 case rests on an unmeasured number.
risk_register.mitigation: Build a wasm32 microbenchmark gate BEFORE locking dispatch/value design; measure real browser engines (V8/SpiderMonkey) and wasmtime; minimize dispatch COUNT via superinstructions; treat a measured browser per-decision number as a hard go/no-go milestone.

risk_register.risk: f64 cross-arch bit-identity breaks via FMA contraction, fast-math, relaxed-SIMD, or libm edge-case divergence native vs wasm32.
risk_register.mitigation: Mandate pure-Rust libm for all transcendentals, ban f64::mul_add/fast-math/relaxed-SIMD, restrict to the IEEE-754 basic op set, canonicalize NaN/-0.0, and pin a single cross-arch golden constant. Provide a fixed-point/Q16.16 escape-hatch build mode for zero-risk determinism.

risk_register.risk: Failing to close the ~29-39x gap on wasm where JIT is unavailable — the interpreter ceiling may not reach the per-tick-per-agent goal in-browser.
risk_register.mitigation: Set MVP = match Luau-in-interpreter (~4x koto -> ~1.0-1.25us); reserve JIT for the native stretch; expose a fuel/LOD knob so leaf cadence is tunable (keep the grabby split: Rust-native hot path + script for cooler leaves) and measure the crossover.

risk_register.risk: The luau-language-spec research stream came back empty (placeholder 'test'); the Luau language surface (metatables, type system, stdlib, vector/buffer/string, weak tables, compat edge cases) is under-researched, risking a frontend/semantics lock-in on incomplete data.
risk_register.mitigation: Commission a dedicated Luau-language-spec research pass as a prerequisite to locking the frontend; use full_moon and the Luau release-727 source as interim oracles; scope MVP to a documented Luau subset and expand against a conformance suite.

risk_register.risk: Native tail-call dispatch depends on nightly `become`/extern "rust-preserve-none" which is unstable and may not emit usefully on wasm32.
risk_register.mitigation: Keep the wasm path on a stable match->br_table loop (never make tail-call load-bearing for wasm); gate the native tail-call dispatch behind a nightly feature with the loop+match as a stable fallback; do not let stabilization timing block the project.

risk_register.risk: Tail-call/threaded dispatch regresses 1.2x-4.6x when compiled to wasm — a wrong universal dispatch choice tanks the priority-#3 target.
risk_register.mitigation: Design opcode handlers once with cfg-conditional dispatch glue (switch-loop on wasm, tail-call on native); microbenchmark the br_table penalty for rustia's actual opcode set before finalizing.

risk_register.risk: Insertion-order requirement interacts badly with inline-cache hidden-class shapes (shape explosion on key delete/re-add, shape-id determinism across VMs).
risk_register.mitigation: Make shapes record insertion order, keep per-VM shape tables, bound shape transitions, and explicitly test delete/re-add sequences against the golden. Keep inline caches speed-only (never observable in values).

risk_register.risk: RC cycle leaks accumulate over long-running sims with thousands of agents holding per-agent state.
risk_register.mitigation: Measure leak rate under representative episodes; add a trial-deletion cycle collector or per-VM heap reset between episodes if needed; consider a per-VM arena that is dropped wholesale at episode boundaries.

risk_register.risk: Snapshot/restore of full script-visible state may be too heavy to capture at SNAPSHOT_EVERY cadence for MP rollback.
risk_register.mitigation: Design value/heap/registers/call-stack layout to be flat and cheaply serializable from day one; fall back to delta or coarse-cadence capture; validate snapshot+restore reproduces the golden bit-for-bit.

risk_register.risk: Copy-and-patch native JIT requires a Rust stencil pipeline that has no off-the-shelf equivalent of Deegen's clang/LLVM build-time tooling.
risk_register.mitigation: Treat JIT as native-only STRETCH; prefer cranelift for the native baseline tier if the stencil pipeline proves too costly; ship a strong interpreter first so the JIT is purely additive.

risk_register.risk: Weak tables and __gc finalizers (if implemented for Luau compat) leak collection timing/order into observable script behavior, breaking determinism.
risk_register.mitigation: If implemented, drive collection/finalization off the deterministic fuel counter with a fixed traversal order, or gate weak tables/__gc out of the deterministic mode entirely.

risk_register.risk: Embedding API drift from koto breaks grabby's drop-in integration.
risk_register.mitigation: Pin the exact consumed koto surface as a compatibility shim and wire rustia behind grabby's Selector trait + Criterion bake-off harness early as a continuous integration gate.

Sources to close: luau.org/library + luau.org/typecheck + /tmp/luau_src VM/src/l*lib.cpp + Ast/Analysis. This blocks frontend, value-model, and determinism-mode decisions; it is a prerequisite, not a parallel pass.

The MVP target (~1.0-1.25us/decision) is extrapolated from script-bench-rs 'Sort Rust objects' (interop/userdata/GC-heavy string quicksort) to grabby's IAUS+SARSA(lambda)+contagion integer-math kernel — near-disjoint VM paths. Cheapest highest-value missing number; collapses the entire extrapolation chain.

No profiling of koto was done — only static source reading + end-to-end timing. The 'dispatch + 24B clone + atomic refcount + RwLock' cost decomposition is inferred from code shape, never measured. SPIKE: cargo-flamegraph/Instruments/perf on koto-int bakeoff at n=5000 for the real per-symbol split (decode/dispatch vs IndexMap FxHash probe vs RwLock lock/unlock vs clone_register vs the actual Q16.16 arithmetic). Without this you cannot rank which of the 5 value/dispatch/GC levers actually pays.

The wasm in-browser tax — the explicitly-named go/no-go gate for priority #3 — has ZERO measurements. Everything (feared 4x, optimistic 1.5-2.5x) is opinion. The mattkeeter tail-call-on-wasm inversion (1.2x-4.6x) is one blog, one VM (Mandelbrot), generalized to architectural fact. SPIKE: build a minimal register-bytecode dispatch microbench (big match->br_table) for grabby's actual opcode mix, compile wasm32, measure ns/dispatch in V8 + SpiderMonkey + wasmtime vs native; do it BEFORE locking dispatch/value design.

Determinism of pure-Rust libm across x86_64-linux + aarch64-mac + wasm32 is ASSERTED ('rapier-proven'), never verified for this exact triple. SPIKE: build libm-0.2.16 sin/cos/exp/pow/log/fmod on all three targets, hash outputs over a dense input sweep, compare bit-for-bit. rapier ships determinism with libm but that does not prove bit-identity across these three specific targets/rounding edge cases. This gates the entire f64-internal-mode bet.

wasm NaN bit-pattern non-determinism is under-treated. The wasm spec makes the sign/payload of NaN results from f64 ops NON-deterministic across engines. Any script f64 op that can yield NaN (0/0, sqrt(neg), inf-inf), then folded via to_bits() into the FNV golden, diverges native-vs-wasm-vs-engine. Brief only mentions -0.0->+0.0 and 'NaN canonicalize' for NaN-boxing. Needs an explicit rule: canonicalize ALL NaNs to one bit pattern at every f64-producing op (not just at hashing), and a test that injects NaN-producing scripts against the golden.

Send-vs-Sync requirement is unverified and load-bearing. hard_constraints demand 'Send + Sync values and whole VM', but the recommended Rc-inside-VM design gives Send-but-NOT-Sync, and grabby's described usage ('N independent VMs, no intra-VM sharing') may only need Send (move owned VM to a pool thread). The console VM is already stored as Bevy NonSend. CHECK grabby's actual thread topology (does any code share &VM across threads, or only move owned VMs?). If only Send is required, the gc-arena/RC fork collapses to 'make the heap Send' and the whole Sync tension partly evaporates. This is verifiable by reading the sim's threadpool/Selector call sites.

'Rc-inside-VM + Send-at-VM-granularity' is presented as nearly free; it actually requires an UNSAFE Send impl on the VM plus an audited invariant that no Rc/Gc handle ever escapes the moved object graph (gluon does exactly this with a per-thread heap). The brief never states this needs unsafe + a soundness argument + miri/loom validation. Concrete: prototype moving a VM holding Rc-heap across pool threads and prove no aliasing under miri before committing the RC direction.

Snapshot/restore of a SUSPENDED VM (reified call stack + open upvalues + closures + heap + native-fn references) is a hard constraint and medium risk, but NO stream investigated how to serialize it. Closures capturing upvalues, interned strings, native function pointers, and inline-cache slots are all hostile to flat serialization. SPIKE: examine whether piccolo/koto can serialize mid-coroutine state at all, and design value/heap/upvalue layout for cheap flat capture from day one; validate snapshot+restore reproduces the golden bit-for-bit.

Per-VM / per-agent MEMORY footprint (priority #2) is never measured and no byte budget exists. The NaN-box-saves-memory axis is argued with no baseline. SPIKE: measure koto-int RSS per VM at 4000 agents (and per-agent Q-table/eligibility-trace size) so the 16B-vs-8B value tradeoff has a real denominator.

call_function entry/exit marshalling cost per agent per tick is unquantified. grabby calls call_function(KValue,&[KValue]) once per agent per tick; at thousands of agents that is thousands of VM entries/tick. SPIKE: microbench an empty koto function call to isolate pure entry overhead, to size whether a batched 'decide N agents per VM call' API is necessary (it is listed as a direction but never costed).

The remaining 74% includes the real in-script arithmetic/map-work that native does in 0.14us — it is NOT shown to be dispatch+boxing overhead. Conflates 'non-FFI cost' with 'VM-dispatch cost'. Needs the koto flamegraph to substantiate the attribution.

'A competent register Luau interpreter is ~4x faster than koto on a realistic interop workload' generalized to 'matching Luau-in-interpreter is the credible MVP (~1.0-1.25us/decision)'. The 4x is a string-sort/userdata benchmark, not the integer-math AI kernel. Unverified that the multiplier transfers; could be larger or much smaller on arithmetic-bound code.

'Deegen/LJR CPS tail-call interpreter +31% over LuaJIT' cited as the SOTA interpreter ceiling for rustia. It is a NATIVE x86 result from an LLVM-build-time meta-compiler, and the +31% rests on the exact tail-call dispatch that INVERTS on wasm. There is no wasm interpreter ceiling number; the relevant in-browser ceiling is unknown and probably far below +31%.

'Tail-call dispatch is 1.2x-4.6x slower on wasm' — single source (one blog, Mandelbrot, one engine set). Treated as universal architectural law. Needs replication on rustia's opcode set/value model before it drives the dispatch design.

'libm is mandatory and bit-identical' AND 'libm is typically slower than system libm' — both asserted without a rustia-relevant measurement of either the bit-identity (across the 3 targets) or the speed penalty on the hot transcendentals grabby uses (the AI kernel may use few/no transcendentals — verify which libm fns are even on the hot path).

'full_moon is too heavy/slow to feed a bytecode compiler' and 'luau-parser is blazingly fast' — both unbenchmarked (one inferred from 'lossless/trivia', the other a crate tagline). Needs a parse-throughput + AST-lowering-cost bench on representative Luau before either is chosen as frontend.

Luau 727 LUA_TINTEGER 'resolves the f64 tension' — the same brief notes integers are NOT folded into hot arith opcodes and are FFlag-gated. So its arithmetic reach is unverified; it may be a host/buffer carrier only. Read /tmp/luau_src VM/src/ltm.cpp + lvmutils.cpp arith paths and the typechecker before relying on it.

'Core f64 +,-,*,/,sqrt are already bit-deterministic cross-arch, no special handling' — true under wasm/IEEE-754 round-to-nearest with no contraction, BUT depends on LLVM never contracting/reassociating and on no NaN production (see NaN gap). Also min/max NaN-propagation semantics differ between IEEE-754-2019, wasm, and Rust f64::min — verify the chosen min/max matches across targets.

'Luau core loop ~16KB fits L1i' is used to justify a 'keep core small' target, but there is no estimate of rustia's size in Rust with target-split dispatch + Q16.16 intrinsics + libm + serde. The L1i claim about Luau-C++ does not transfer as a target without a rustia-specific number.

koto per-decision headline '5.4us' vs README table (1k = 6.40ms = 6.4us). Minor but the canonical number should be pinned; the brief repeats 5.4 without noting the table's 6.4 at the smallest n (cache/warmup effects unexamined).
missing_directions: Fork/embed Luau-the-C++-VM compiled to wasm rather than building from scratch. This is the single biggest unexamined alternative: mlua+Luau is ALREADY at the 4x MVP target today. The brief dismisses it as 'C bindings, not wasm-clean' but never verifies whether Luau (C++) can compile to wasm (it ships in browsers via Roblox/emscripten) and link into a wasm-bindgen/Bevy host, nor whether determinism (libm swap + add instruction-fuel via SingleStep) + Send could be retrofitted. The real blocker is likely wasm32-unknown-unknown having no libc (needs wasi/emscripten) and Send/Sync — but that must be a verified spike, not an assumption, because it could save the entire from-scratch effort.

Data-oriented / batched SoA execution: process all N agents' decisions in one VM invocation over struct-of-arrays state, amortizing dispatch and entry overhead across agents. Listed once in the grabby stream's candidate directions but never elevated to a design axis despite directly attacking the per-call marshalling and dispatch-count problems that dominate at thousands of agents.

Type-specialized / typed-subset compilation. Luau already has type-guided bytecode type-info driving native codegen. A direction where rustia compiles a TYPED Luau subset (the hot AI kernel is small, known, monomorphic) to specialized straight-line bytecode or closure-tree — getting much of the JIT win on wasm WITHOUT a JIT — is absent. The brief commits to a general dynamic interpreter and treats perf purely as dispatch/value tuning.

Compile-the-known-kernel-to-Rust-closures-at-load (partial evaluation against the specific scenario/considerations). The hot script is tiny and structurally fixed (4 considerations x 6 actions); specializing it at load into a closure tree with constants folded could approach native, works on wasm, and is more concrete than the generic 'closure/threaded-code' direction.

Explicit treatment of the 'don't run script every agent every tick' option as a first-class direction. The ai_bakeoff VERDICT already concluded: keep the hot kernel in Rust, script only cooler leaves. rustia's value case may NOT be the per-tick hot path at all — it may be the cooler/coarser layer where koto already suffices, which would radically change the perf bar. The brief never revisits whether the per-tick-per-agent target is even the right goal given grabby's own measured verdict.

Cranelift-as-the-only-JIT-tier (skip copy-and-patch entirely) with the explicit cost/benefit, plus whether cranelift itself works/links on the native targets without bloating the wasm build. Brief mentions cranelift as a fallback but never explores it as the primary native tier with its own tradeoff analysis.

Interning + small-string-optimization as its own axis. Flagged as 'low-hanging fruit' in koto-internals but never made a design direction with a sizing of how much of grabby's cost is string-related (likely little, given float-free integer kernel — which itself argues the SSO win is small and should be deprioritized; that inversion is unexamined).
critic.verdict: NOT sufficient to start the 5-way design exploration. The brief is strong on koto internals, Luau VM internals, and the SOTA-VM landscape, but three load-bearing pillars are unmeasured assumption, and one entire input stream is empty. Fill these FIRST: (1) the luau-language-spec stream must actually be run — metatables, type system, stdlib, vector/buffer/string libs, weak tables, __gc, and determinism surfaces (string.format, next() order, math.random) gate the frontend and value/number model that the design exploration is supposed to choose between. (2) Three cheap, decisive spikes must produce real numbers before locking architecture: (a) port the ai_bakeoff kernel to Luau and measure us/decision under mlua (validates the MVP target and the '4x' claim on the ACTUAL workload, not a string sort); (b) a wasm32 dispatch microbench in V8/SpiderMonkey/wasmtime (the named go/no-go gate, currently 100% extrapolated); (c) a libm bit-identity check across x86_64-linux + aarch64-mac + wasm32 (gates the f64-internal mode). (3) Resolve the Send-vs-Sync question by reading grabby's actual thread topology — it materially changes the GC/RC decision and may dissolve the gc-arena tension. (4) Profile koto (flamegraph) to replace the inferred '74% is dispatch+boxing' attribution with measured per-symbol costs, so the value/dispatch/GC axes can be ranked. Additionally, add two missing directions to the exploration set before it starts: 'embed/fork Luau-C++-to-wasm vs from-scratch' (the unexamined alternative that could obviate the project) and 'batched SoA / typed-subset specialization' (the directions that actually attack per-agent dispatch+marshalling at thousands of agents). Until the empty stream is filled and spikes (a)-(c) return numbers, the design exploration would be choosing between five options on top of an unmeasured foundation.

result.summary: koto 0.16.1 is a register-based bytecode VM (NOT tree-walking) with a two-level dispatch: InstructionReader::next() decodes a variable-length byte stream into a 169-variant Instruction enum returned by value, which execute_instruction then matches in a single giant match (LLVM jump table, no computed-goto/threading). Pipeline is koto_lexer -> koto_parser (AST) -> koto_bytecode::Compiler -> Chunk{bytes:Vec<u8>, constants}. Values are a 24-byte KValue enum; numbers are a tagged i64/f64 KNumber (koto HAS an integer subtype, unlike Luau f64-only). Memory is pure reference counting with NO tracing GC and NO cycle detection (cycles leak); default feature is `rc` (Rc+RefCell), grabby's required `arc` feature makes every heap value an Arc and every mutable container an Arc<parking_lot::RwLock<T>>, so each map/list/object touch pays an atomic refcount bump plus a RwLock lock/unlock. Maps are insertion-ordered IndexMap<ValueKey,KValue,FxHasher> (a good deterministic model to copy). The big perf sinks are double dispatch + varint decode per op, 24-byte KValue clones bumping atomic refcounts on the hot path, RwLock-guarded container access under arc, per-call Frame push + register Vec resize(fill Null/drop), and always-heap strings. Critically, koto's only execution limit is WALL-CLOCK Duration (Instant::now), not deterministic instruction-count fuel, and there is no recursion-depth limit — both are hard gaps rustia must fill.

key_findings.finding: Register-based bytecode VM. Two-stage dispatch: InstructionReader (koto_bytecode/instruction_reader.rs:22 Iterator::next) decodes a byte stream into a 169-variant `Instruction` enum (built and returned by value each step), then KotoVm::execute_instruction (koto_runtime/vm.rs:740) matches that enum. Driving loop execute_instructions (vm.rs:674) `while let Some(instruction) = self.reader.next()`. No threaded/computed-goto dispatch; relies on the Rust match compiling to a jump table. Operands are varint-decoded (get_var_u32) per instruction.

koto_lexer -> koto_parser (AST) -> koto_bytecode::Compiler (compiler.rs, 4470 lines) -> Chunk { bytes: Vec<u8>, constants: ConstantPool } (chunk.rs:50). Bytecode-compiled, not tree-walking. 93 real opcodes (Op enum indices 0..=92; 94..255 are Unused placeholders) in op.rs, but 169 Instruction enum variants because some ops fan out (SetNumberU8/SetNumberNegU8 -> SetNumber, SetTrue/SetFalse -> SetBool).

KValue (types/value.rs:11) is a 13-variant enum: Null,Bool,Number(KNumber),Range,List,Tuple,Map,Str,Function,NativeFunction,Iterator,Object,TemporaryTuple. A unit test asserts size_of::<KValue>() <= 24. KFunction is the only 24-byte variant and carries an explicit `_niche: Niche` field so the compiler can niche-pack the KValue tag into it. All other payloads are <=16 bytes.

KNumber (types/number.rs:14) is `enum { F64(f64), I64(i64) }` (16 bytes). koto HAS a native integer subtype — directly relevant to the Luau-is-f64-only tension. Every arithmetic op is a 4-way match over (lhs,rhs) int/float combos; integer ops use wrapping_* ; Div always promotes to f64. Hash uses to_bits(); Eq/Ord compare cross-type by casting i64->f64.

KString (koto_parser/string.rs:20) is 16 bytes: enum Inner { Full(Ptr<String>), Slice(StringSlice<u16>) inline, SliceLarge(Ptr<StringSlice<usize>>) }. Backed by Arc<String> (under arc) with shared zero-copy subslicing via byte bounds. NO small-string inline optimization — even 1-char strings heap-allocate. String concat (run_add, vm.rs:1638) does `a.to_string() + b` -> fresh allocation.

KMap (types/map.rs:63) = { data: PtrMut<ValueMap>, meta: Option<PtrMut<MetaMap>> } = 16 bytes. ValueMap = IndexMap<ValueKey, KValue, BuildHasherDefault<FxHasher>>. Insertion order from indexmap (deterministic); hashing by rustc_hash::FxHasher (seedless, deterministic). ValueKey wraps a KValue, constructible only from hashable variants. Excellent deterministic model for rustia to copy.

KList = PtrMut<SmallVec<[KValue;4]>> (8 bytes; inline for <=4 elems). KFunction (types/function.rs:11) = chunk:Ptr<Chunk>, ip:u32, arg_count/optional_arg_count:u8, flags, context:Option<Ptr<FunctionContext>> holding captures (a KList) + non_locals. Closures capture by mutating a shared KList after creation. KNativeFunction = Ptr<dyn KotoFunction> (16-byte fat pointer); KotoFunction = Fn(&mut CallContext)->Result<KValue> + Send + Sync + 'static.

koto_memory/lib.rs explicitly: 'only reference-counted pointers without cycle detection'. NO tracing GC. Ptr<T> = Arc<T> (arc) or Rc<T> (rc). PtrMut<T> = Ptr<KCell<T>>; KCell = parking_lot::RwLock<T> under arc (arc/ptr_mut.rs:38) or RefCell<T> under rc. Reference cycles LEAK. Default feature is rc+serde (koto Cargo.toml); grabby must use arc for Send+Sync.

Under arc every container read/mutation goes through Arc<parking_lot::RwLock>. KMap::data()=self.0.borrow()=RwLock::read(); list/object access likewise. A single map lookup costs: Arc deref + atomic refcount (if cloned) + RwLock read-lock acquire/release + IndexMap FxHash probe. clone() of any heap KValue variant is an ATOMIC increment under arc vs non-atomic under rc.

The ONLY execution limit is wall-clock: KotoVmSettings.execution_limit: Option<Duration> (vm.rs:90). ExecutionTimeout (vm.rs:3928) batches Instant::now() checks (recalibrated to ~1/10 of the limit). NON-deterministic, unusable for grabby's bit-for-bit fuel. NO instruction-count cap and NO recursion-depth limit (recursion bounded only by native stack / call_stack Vec -> can overflow). The check_for_timeout() branch runs once per instruction in the hot loop.

call_koto_function (vm.rs:2923) + push_frame (vm.rs:3444): clones chunk Ptr (atomic refcount under arc), pushes a Frame (chunk Ptr, Option<NonLocals>, register_base, return ips, catch_stack:Vec, execution_barrier) onto call_stack Vec, resizes the shared registers:Vec<KValue> filling with KValue::Null on NewFrame (vm.rs:751) and again on pop_frame (vm.rs:3505), dropping old values. apply_optional/variadic/captures run per call. No inline caching, no arg-count specialization.

Registers live in one Vm-wide Vec<KValue> indexed by register_base+reg. set_register/get_register are bounds-checked Vec indexing (vm.rs:3565,3583). `Copy` op and every Call/Return do clone_register (full 24-byte KValue clone -> refcount bump for heap variants). Binary ops read operands by reference but each writes a moved result. No NaN-boxing; values are a fat tagged union moved/cloned around.

implications_for_rustia: API surface to MATCH for drop-in: a Koto-like handle with compile()->chunk + run + call_function; a KValue-like enum; native fns as Fn(&mut Ctx)->Result<Value> with ctx.args()->&[Value]; prelude/exports as maps; serde bridge. These are koto touchpoints grabby already depends on.

Insertion-ordered IndexMap + seedless FxHash is the determinism win to copy verbatim: keep it (or a custom insertion-ordered open-addressing map) and never use RandomState/SipHash. We inherit bit-for-bit map ordering for free.

koto's wall-clock execution_limit is unusable for determinism. rustia MUST implement a deterministic instruction-count fuel counter decremented in the dispatch loop, plus a separate recursion/call-depth cap. This is a required feature koto entirely lacks — a clear must-have differentiator.

~74% of cost is the interpreted VM, not FFI (grabby's ~26% finding). The payoff is in execution-engine quality (dispatch, value boxing, no per-container lock), not the embedding boundary; optimizing FFI alone caps at ~26%.

Two-level dispatch (decode-to-enum then match) is wasteful: fuse decode+execute via fixed-width encoding read in-loop, closure/tail-call threading, or computed-goto. Stop building a 169-variant Instruction enum by value every step.

24-byte cloned tagged union + atomic refcounts dominate the hot path. Consider NaN-boxing (8-byte values) so int/float/bool/null/short-strings are Copy and need no refcount; reserve heap-pointer payloads for the rest, directly attacking clone_register churn on Copy/Call/Return.

arc = Arc<RwLock> tax with ZERO contention in grabby's N-independent-VM model. Since VMs don't share state intra-VM, rustia can be Send+Sync at VM granularity (move whole VM across threads) while using non-atomic Rc + Cell/RefCell interior mutability INSIDE a VM — eliminating both atomic refcounts and RwLock locks. Single biggest structural win over koto-arc.

koto has an i64 subtype but Luau is f64-only. Full Luau compat inherits f64-only, colliding with grabby's int/Q16.16 float-free boundary. Explore a hidden integer-tagged fast path (LuaJIT/koto-style dual-number) or expose Q16.16 host types at the boundary while keeping f64 internally. Central semantic tension to flag.
Strings always heap-allocate: add inline small-string optimization and/or interning for map keys/identifiers. koto's lack of SSO is low-hanging fruit for speed and memory.

Call setup resizes a shared register Vec with Null-fill on every call and return: use register windows / a pre-sized stack without per-call fill-and-drop, borrow (not clone) the chunk pointer per call, and add inline caching for field/method access (koto has none).
candidate_directions: Direction A — 'koto-shaped but faster': keep register bytecode + insertion-ordered IndexMap + tagged-enum values, but fuse dispatch (computed-goto/threaded), add NaN-boxing, deterministic fuel, and Rc-inside-VM (Send at VM granularity). Lowest-risk, highest-compat with grabby's integration.

Direction B — 'NaN-boxed register VM + native JIT': 8-byte NaN-boxed values, a baseline template/cranelift JIT on native for hot functions, interpreter fallback on wasm. Maximizes the 'within a small multiple of native' prize natively while staying viable in-browser.

Direction C — 'full Luau front-end, custom backend': implement the real Luau lexer/parser/compiler (latest-Luau compat) but emit rustia's own deterministic register bytecode rather than Luau's VM, getting compat + control over determinism/fuel.

Direction D — 'lock-free Send+Sync via VM-per-thread ownership': abandon Arc<RwLock> entirely; make the whole VM Send (move across pool threads) with single-threaded interior mutability, eliminating all per-borrow atomic/lock tax — the structural fix for grabby's N-VM workload.

Direction E — 'closure/threaded-code interpreter': compile bytecode to a tree of boxed Rust closures (or tail-called fn pointers) at load time, eliminating per-op decode and enum-build; deterministic fuel via a counter threaded through closures. Middle ground between bytecode-interpret and JIT that works on wasm.
open_questions: Exact measured size_of for KValue under each feature (rc vs arc) and real per-op ns cost — needs building koto with a microbenchmark; the <=24-byte figure is a compile-time assert, not a measured layout.
Does NaN-boxing's loss of an i64 subtype matter for grabby? koto keeps i64; Luau f64-only + grabby's fixed-point boundary needs a concrete reconciliation design.
How does parking_lot::RwLock behave on wasm32-unknown-unknown (spin fallback, atomics-feature requirement)? Quantify the actual arc tax in-browser vs native.
What fraction of grabby's ~5us is map lookups vs arithmetic vs call overhead? Needs a per-opcode profile of a real grabby decision script to prioritize rustia's optimizations.
Can rustia guarantee bit-for-bit f64 determinism across native and wasm32 given FMA/rounding differences? koto sidesteps this by grabby keeping all f64 math in Rust; in-script f64 reopens this risk.

Is full latest-Luau compat compatible with a non-Luau bytecode/value model, or must we track Luau VM semantics (metatables, vector type, buffer library) closely enough that reusing Luau's own compiler is cheaper?

result.summary: The Rust scripting landscape splits into pure-Rust engines (koto, rhai, rune, steel, gluon, hematita, dyon, piccolo) and bindings to C/C++ VMs (mlua/rlua → PUC-Lua/LuaJIT/Luau). On the only apples-to-apples interop benchmark (script-bench-rs, "Sort Rust objects": quicksort of 10k userdata-wrapped random strings, M5 Max), mlua+Luau runs in 11.94 ms while koto 0.16.1 takes 49.21 ms and rhai 114.27 ms — i.e. the official Luau interpreter is ~4x faster than koto and ~9.6x faster than rhai on a realistic, interop-heavy game-like workload. This is the single most important number: it both sets rustia's perf bar (beat/match Luau-in-interpreter) and proves koto leaves ~4x on the table. The two most directly reusable assets are (1) piccolo's gc-arena (safe incremental GC via generativity + mutate-xor-collect) and stackless/fuel VM architecture, which map almost exactly onto rustia's steppable-fuel + recursion-limit requirements, and (2) full_moon, a lossless multi-dialect-including-Luau parser with error recovery. The hard blocker: gc-arena is fundamentally single-threaded and NOT Send/Sync, colliding with the "N independent Send+Sync VMs across a thread pool" constraint. koto solves Send via a compile-time Rc↔Arc feature swap and — critically for determinism — uses a dual I64/F64 number type, unlike Luau's f64-only numbers. mlua is the API-ergonomics gold standard (UserData, FromLua/IntoLua, Scope, async-over-coroutines) and should be the embedding-API model.

key_findings.finding: Pure-Rust Lua VM, register-based bytecode modeled on PUC-Rio Lua 5.3/5.4. 'Stackless'/trampoline design: the call stack is reified into an Executor object polled via Executor::step(fuel). Rust callbacks return either an immediate result or a Sequence (a Future-like multi-step object the Executor drives). Never uses the Rust call stack for Lua->Rust->Lua nesting, making it DoS-resilient against untrusted scripts. This is architecturally near-identical to rustia's steppable/fuel requirement.

Safe incremental, cycle-detecting mark-sweep GC modeled on PUC Lua 5.3/5.4. Gc<'gc,T> pointers are machine-word-sized, Copy, zero-cost (no write barriers on mutation). Safety via generative lifetimes (the 'gc brand) + a Collect derive trait. Core invariant 'mutate XOR collect': all Gc access happens inside Arena::mutate closures that must RETURN before collection runs (proving no Gc lives on the Rust stack) — this invariant is precisely WHY piccolo had to become stackless. Tracks all arena memory for fuel/budget. Used in production by Ruffle (Flash emulator). Dual MIT/CC0.

gc-arena has NO support for multi-threaded allocation/collection; Arena and Gc are NOT Send and NOT Sync by design. Gc pointers are raw, unsynchronized. This directly conflicts with rustia's 'N independent Send+Sync VMs across a thread pool' constraint. Mitigation paths: (a) keep each VM strictly thread-local and move work, not VMs (loses koto's arc model); (b) make the whole Arena Send-but-not-Sync so a VM can be migrated between threads (requires all interior types Send and no thread-local state — non-trivial, upstream does not guarantee it); (c) adopt gc-arena's safe-GC IDEA but build a Send-capable arena ourselves.

Experimental, pre-1.0 (v0.3.x). Core language + register VM feature-complete; most stdlib, finalization, debug lib, stack traces unimplemented. Author explicitly says bytecode/interp loop are unoptimized and NOT competitive with LuaJIT/Luau yet ('not very good at fast interpreter loops yet'). Uses some unsafe to keep Value small (avoid fat pointers). Compiles to and runs in WASM (the blog ships in-browser REPLs). Lua 5.x semantics, NOT Luau — would need Luau syntax/semantics retrofit.

key_findings.topic: Luau VM (via mlua) — perf bar and compat target
key_findings.finding: Official Luau is the fastest realistic option here: 11.94 ms vs koto 49.21 ms (~4.1x). Luau interpreter is roughly as fast as LuaJIT 2.1 *interpreter* mode; with partial native codegen it is ~1.6x slower than LuaJIT JIT. Register-based bytecode, multi-pass compiler (AST->bytecode with optimization passes), dispatch loop inspired by LuaJIT, core loop ~16KB on x64 (fits I-cache). Luau numbers are f64-only (no integer subtype). This is the C++ reference implementation rustia must match in interpreter mode and stay compatible with.

Lossless parser for Lua 5.1/5.2/5.3/5.4 AND Luau (LuaVersion flag), by Kampfkarren. Preserves all trivia (comments/whitespace) for exact round-trip; error recovery via AstResult that always yields an Ast even on syntax errors. Actively maintained (v2.x), battle-tested as the frontend for StyLua and selene. Trade-off: lossless/trivia-rich AST is built for tooling (formatters/linters), so it is heavier and slower than a perf-oriented parser and the AST shape is not ideal to feed straight into a bytecode compiler. Usable as a correctness oracle / initial frontend; likely want a trivia-stripping pass or eventually a custom lexer+parser for speed.

Bindings (not pure Rust) to Lua 5.1-5.5/LuaJIT/Luau. API is the gold standard: UserData trait (add_method/add_method_mut/add_field/add_meta_method), FromLua/IntoLua + multi-value variants (auto IntoLua, manual FromLua), Scope for registering non-'static borrowed Rust data safely, UserDataRef/UserDataRefMut borrow guards, blanket UserData impls for Rc/Arc/Rc<RefCell<T>>/Arc<Mutex<T>>, registry, async/await implemented over Lua coroutines (Future polled; Poll::Pending -> coroutine yield). rustia should mirror this surface for embedding.

Register-based bytecode VM (instructions carry u8 register operands; KValue has a TemporaryTuple/RegisterSlice optimization). Value is a Clone enum KValue { Null,Bool,Number(KNumber),Range,List,Tuple,Map,Str,Function,NativeFunction,Iterator,Object,TemporaryTuple }. KNumber is a dual enum { F64(f64), I64(i64) } — already has an integer subtype, directly relevant to the determinism/float-free-boundary tension. Send achieved by compile-time feature swap: koto_memory exposes Ptr as Rc (feature 'rc') or Arc (feature 'arc'); KotoSend/KotoSync are empty blanket traits under 'rc' and re-exports of std Send/Sync under 'arc'. Reference-counted (no tracing GC) — leaks cycles but is simple and WASM-clean.

AST tree-walking interpreter (NO bytecode). Slowest in the benchmark at 114.27 ms (~2.3x slower than koto, ~9.6x slower than Luau); author states ~2x slower than CPython and that speed is explicitly not the goal. Optimizations: small packed AST/runtime structs for cache-friendliness, hash-based function dispatch. Pure Rust, reference-counted, mature, excellent docs, strong embedding ergonomics, good WASM support, optional sync feature. Relevant only as an API/ergonomics reference and a 'what not to do for perf' (tree-walking) data point.

Pure-Rust, stack-based bytecode VM. Reference-counted memory; dynamic Value container; first-class async + generators; claims multithreaded execution support with a SyncFunction type (Send-capable function handle). serde-friendly containers out of the box. Not in the benchmark. Stack VM is simpler but generally slower per-op than register VM. Useful reference for async + Send function design and for embedding API.

Embeddable Scheme (R5RS-ish, R7RS underway) implemented as a bytecode VM, by mattwparas. Engine is explicitly NOT Send or Sync — disqualifying for rustia's threading model without rework. Good native Rust interop + FFI. Not Lua-compatible (Scheme), so low direct relevance beyond VM-design study.

Statically-typed, type-inferred functional language (ML-like) in Rust, tracing GC with a SEPARATE small heap per gluon thread (keeps GC overhead low and is the closest existing model to 'one heap per VM'). Rust thread-safety guaranteed. Low-boilerplate marshalling. Not Lua/dynamic, niche, slower-moving. Relevant mainly for its per-thread-heap GC architecture idea.

Pure-Rust Lua interpreter (lexer->parser->bytecode compiler->VM) in 100% SAFE Rust, no unsafe, minimal deps, stable compiler — goal is a hardened/secure Lua. Largely abandoned/early, incomplete Lua coverage, not perf-focused. Low relevance except as a safe-only reference.

Piston's dynamically-typed game scripting language. NO garbage collector — uses a Rust-like lifetime/borrow checker plus copy-on-write instead. Novel but idiosyncratic semantics, not Lua-compatible, low activity. Relevant only as an alternative-to-GC memory-management idea.

Pure-Rust JavaScript engine. In the benchmark 101.87 ms (~2x slower than koto, ~8.5x slower than Luau). JS, not Lua; heavier semantics. Relevant only as a pure-Rust dynamic-VM engineering reference (it has a real bytecode VM + GC, boa_gc).

wasmoon is Lua compiled to WASM via Emscripten exposed to JS — a browser JS library, not a Rust embedding crate; not relevant to a Rust host. The benchmark's wasmtime (2.73 ms) and wasmi (10.02 ms) rows represent precompiled Rust-to-WASM, i.e. a near-native ceiling, not a scripting language — they show the cost floor of a WASM-interpreter approach (wasmi 10ms) vs JIT (wasmtime 2.7ms, no JIT in browser).
rlua is now a thin wrapper re-export over mlua (merged); treat as mlua for all purposes. Not pure Rust.

implications_for_rustia: The benchmark proves the thesis: a competent register-based Luau bytecode interpreter (mlua_luau, 11.94ms) is ~4x faster than koto (49.21ms) on interop-heavy workloads. rustia's MVP target should be 'match Luau-in-interpreter,' which alone would take grabby from ~4-5us to ~1.0-1.25us/decision. Tree-walking (rhai) is categorically disqualified for the perf bar.

gc-arena is the most attractive GC design (safe, incremental, zero-cost Copy pointers, memory-tracked for fuel) AND its mutate-xor-collect invariant naturally forces the exact stackless/steppable VM rustia needs. BUT it is hard-not-Send/Sync. This is the central architectural fork: either (a) adopt gc-arena and accept thread-local VMs (migrate work, not VMs), (b) attempt to make a single Arena Send-but-not-Sync for VM migration, or (c) reject tracing GC in favor of koto's proven Rc↔Arc-feature-swap reference counting (Send via 'arc' feature, no cycle collection).

koto's KNumber { I64, F64 } dual representation is the template for rustia's determinism story: keep an integer subtype internally even though Luau spec is f64-only. This lets the host<->script boundary stay int/Q16.16 and avoids f64 nondeterminism for integer-domain work, at the cost of Luau-compat nuance (Luau scripts assume f64 semantics — rustia must define exactly when a value is I64 vs F64 and ensure bit-identical results native vs wasm32).

full_moon is a viable correctness-oracle and initial Luau frontend (lossless, error-recovery, real Luau coverage, maintained, used by StyLua/selene), but its trivia-heavy lossless AST is built for tooling and is too heavy/slow to feed a bytecode compiler directly. Plan: use it to bootstrap/validate, but budget for a trivia-stripping lowering pass or an eventual purpose-built lexer+parser for compile speed.

mlua defines the embedding-API target surface: UserData (methods/meta-methods/fields), FromLua/IntoLua (+multi), Scope for non-'static borrows, UserDataRef guards, blanket impls over Rc/Arc wrappers, async-over-coroutines. rustia's Rust API should be a near-clone of this, adjusted so handles are Send under the 'arc'-equivalent build.

piccolo's Sequence/Executor::step(fuel) model gives steppable fuel + recursion limits and DoS resilience essentially for free and is deterministic (fuel measured in VM instructions, not wall-clock) — exactly matching grabby's deterministic-fuel requirement. The cost is ergonomic: native callbacks that re-enter the VM must be written as Sequences (poll-style), not straight-line Rust. rustia should budget for this complexity if it adopts the stackless design.

WASM ceiling data (wasmi 10ms interp, wasmtime 2.7ms JIT) confirms JIT is the real prize but is moot in-browser; rustia should architect the interpreter to be the primary, always-available path (Luau's philosophy) and treat native JIT as an optional native-only accelerator, not the baseline.
candidate_directions: Direction A — Fork/port piccolo: adopt gc-arena + stackless register VM wholesale, retrofit Luau syntax (via full_moon frontend) and Luau semantics, accept thread-local VMs. Fastest path to a safe, fuel-native VM but inherits piccolo's immaturity, unoptimized interp loop, and the Send problem.

Direction B — koto-style pragmatism, faster: build a fresh register VM with an enum Value + Rc↔Arc feature swap (Send solved like koto) and dual I64/F64 numbers (determinism solved like koto), but invest in a Luau-grade dispatch loop (computed-goto-equivalent, small bytecode, I-cache-tight) to close koto's 4x gap to Luau. No tracing GC (RC + leak cycles, or add a small cycle collector later).

Direction C — Transliterate the Luau C++ VM to Rust: port Luau's actual bytecode format, compiler passes, and dispatch loop to Rust for guaranteed compat + proven perf, layering rustia's determinism (I64 subtype, fixed-point boundary), fuel stepping, and Send model on top. Highest compat fidelity, highest effort, must reconcile Luau's f64-only model with determinism.

Direction D — gc-arena GC + bespoke Send wrapper: keep gc-arena's safe incremental GC but engineer the Arena to be Send (thread-local during execution, migratable between steps) to satisfy 'N VMs across a thread pool.' Highest-risk on the GC/threading axis but best-of-both on memory + safety.

Direction E — full_moon frontend + custom bytecode backend as a deliberate split: reuse full_moon (or luau-parser) for parsing/error-recovery only, then build a clean register-bytecode compiler+VM with whichever GC/threading model wins. De-risks the parser (hardest-to-get-right-for-compat) while keeping the perf-critical VM fully in our control.
open_questions: Is gc-arena's Arena makeable Send (not Sync) without forking the crate — i.e. can a whole VM be moved between pool threads between steps? Need to read gc-arena 0.5.x source for the exact auto-trait situation and whether the 'gc brand and internal Cells block Send.
What is piccolo's actual interpreter-loop throughput today vs koto and vs Luau? No published number exists; needs a direct micro-benchmark before betting on Direction A.

How do we reconcile Luau's f64-only number spec with a deterministic I64 subtype? Does grabby's float-free boundary mean rustia can legally deviate from Luau number semantics internally, or must observable script behavior match Luau bit-for-bit (which f64 already makes nondeterministic across platforms unless we pin f64 ops)?

full_moon parse throughput and AST-lowering cost — is it fast enough for runtime script loading, or only for offline compile? Need a benchmark on representative Luau sources, plus comparison to luau-parser (claims 'blazingly fast').
Does mlua's async-over-coroutines model translate to a Send+Sync world, and is async even needed for grabby's per-agent AI (likely no — synchronous stepped execution suffices)?

Cycle collection: can rustia tolerate RC cycle leaks (koto does) given long-running game sims with thousands of agents, or is a tracing/cycle collector mandatory — which then re-raises the gc-arena Send problem?
Determinism of any tracing GC: does collection timing/order ever leak into observable script behavior (finalizer order, weak-table semantics)? Luau weak tables + __gc would be a determinism hazard.
