result.summary: Analyzed luau-lang/luau release 727 (commit f1f121d, 2026-06-26) source directly plus the official luau.org/performance doc. Luau is a register-based bytecode VM (32-bit fixed-width instructions) with a portable C interpreter using computed-goto dispatch on GCC/Clang and falling back to a switch on MSVC. It deliberately does NOT NaN-box: TValue is 16 bytes (8-byte Value union + 4-byte extra + 4-byte tag) to hold doubles, 64-bit pointers AND a native 3-float vector. Its speed comes from a stack of mutually-reinforcing tricks: self-patching inline caches on field/method access, load-time import resolution, a FASTCALL path that calls 133 C builtins without a Lua call frame, hybrid array+hash tables with a cached length boundary, an incremental NON-generational NON-moving mark&sweep GC with Go-style allocation-driven (not wall-clock) pacing, and an IR-based type-guided native code generator (x64/A64) with deopt-to-bytecode fallback. CRITICAL UPDATE for rustia: release 727 has added an int64 integer subtype (LUA_TINTEGER, lua_pushinteger64, behind FFlags LuauIntegerType2/LuauIntegerFastcalls) plus native classes — directly relevant to the f64-determinism tension. For wasm32 the two biggest native tricks (computed goto, runtime native codegen) do not survive, which makes interpreter-dispatch quality and value-representation the dominant levers in-browser.

key_findings.finding: Register-based VM with fixed 32-bit instructions: byte0=opcode(0xff), then either three 8-bit register operands A/B/C, or signed D (insn>>16) / E (insn>>8); some ops consume a following 32-bit AUX word (LUAU_INSN_* macros in Common/include/Luau/Bytecode.h:460-484). Bytecode versions: LBC_VERSION target 7 (min 3, max 11); type-info version target 3. Register model means ~20-50% fewer dispatched instructions than Lua 5.0-style stack VM for typical expressions.

VM_USE_CGOTO=1 for __GNUC__/__clang__ (lvmexecute.cpp:122-138): VM_NEXT() = goto*(kDispatchTable[op]) with a 256-entry label table; MSVC path degrades to a switch. SingleStep mode forces a per-instruction dispatch label so steppable execution coexists with computed goto. The per-opcode indirect-branch sites are what give the CPU BTB per-opcode specialization.

TValue = {Value value (8B union: GCObject* gc / void* p / double n / int64_t l / float v[2]); int extra[LUA_EXTRA_SIZE]; int tt;} = 16 bytes on 64-bit (lobject.h:32-51, luaconf.h:136-140). Vector is first-class: v[0],v[1] in the union and v[2] in extra (LUA_VECTOR_SIZE=3 => EXTRA=1). Luau explicitly rejects NaN-boxing because it must store full 64-bit doubles, 64-bit pointers, and the vector simultaneously.

Luau now has LUA_TINTEGER (lua.h:77), carried in Value.l (int64_t), with API lua_pushinteger64/lua_tointeger64 (lapi.cpp), VM equality on integers (lvmexecute.cpp:1452), and compiler support: Constant::Type_Integer folding (ConstantFolding.cpp:47, BuiltinFolding.cpp:86), an 'integer' builtin library and buffer readinteger/writeinteger, gated by FFlags LuauIntegerType2 / LuauIntegerFastcalls / LuauIntegerBufferFastcalls. Arithmetic fast-paths (LOP_ADD etc.) still only special-case f64 'number' and vector; integers currently flow as a distinct carrier type, not yet folded into the hot arith opcodes.

Single-entry inline cache embedded in the bytecode: the instruction's C byte is a cached LuaNode slot index, masked by table->nodemask8 (lvmexecute.cpp:512). Fast path: if node.key string pointer == constant key pointer (interned identity compare) and value non-nil, return it in 1 compare. On miss without metatable it does luaH_getstr then self-patches the C byte via VM_PATCH_C(pc-2, cachedslot) (lines 524-542). Same scheme for SETTABLEKS, NAMECALL, and (new) userdata direct-field handlers (udatadirectfields, GETUDATAKS/NAMECALLUDATA).

GETIMPORT (lvmexecute.cpp:476-495) pre-resolves dotted global chains (e.g. math.max, string.format) into the proto constant table k at load time; runtime fast path is a single constant load guarded by cl->env->safeenv. Optimization is disabled when the environment is mutated via getfenv/setfenv/loadstring (safeenv flag).

LOP_FASTCALL/FASTCALL1/2/2K/3 (lvmexecute.cpp:3004-3051) invoke a luau_FastFunction from luauF_table[bfid] directly on registers, skipping Lua call-frame setup; on success it jumps past the function-load + CALL instructions. Guarded by safeenv; returns -1 to bail to the normal CALL path. There are 133 LBF_ builtin ids (Bytecode.h) covering math/bit32/string/table/buffer/vector. This is the main reason builtin-heavy code approaches native speed.

Hybrid array+hash (lobject.h LuaTable): array part (sizearray) + closed-addressing hash of LuaNode{TValue val; TKey key;} (32 bytes/node). lsizenode=log2(node count), nodemask8 for fast masking; union lastfree/aboundary caches the negated '#t' boundary. Guarantees element at #t lives in the array part. Length uses a branch-free binary search (luau.org: '50+% faster'). No general shape/hidden-class system — the inline cache + interned-key identity gives most of the hidden-class benefit for fixed-field-name access patterns.

lgc.cpp:24 states verbatim: 'incremental non-generational non-moving mark&sweep'. States: GCSpause, GCSpropagate, GCSpropagateagain (the 'remark' phase to cut atomic cost), GCSatomic, then sweep (lgc.h:19-22). Pacing is allocation-driven via a Go-inspired controller: GCthreshold/heaptrigger computed from gcgoal, gcstepmul, gcstepsize plus an integral error offset getheaptriggererroroffset (lgc.cpp:1133-1240). Paged sweeper is 2-3x faster than linked-list sweep and saves 16 bytes/object. Generational GC discussed in blog posts is experimental, NOT the shipped default.

IR-based pipeline (CodeGen/src): bytecode -> typed IR -> x64 (AssemblyBuilderX64) or A64 (AssemblyBuilderA64). Type-guided lowering emits CHECK_TAG guards with per-pc fallbackBlock() deopt that re-enters the bytecode interpreter on guard failure (IrTranslation.cpp:45-191). Uses the compiler's bytecode type-info (LBC_TYPE_VERSION up to 3). It is a method-JIT/templated lowering, not a tracing JIT; typical native speedup is ~2x over the interpreter, far short of a full optimizing JIT — and it is entirely unavailable on wasm32.

At -O2: constant folding incl. across locals and builtin calls with constant args (ConstantFolding.cpp, BuiltinFolding.cpp, with Type_Integer constants), builtin recognition into FASTCALL, local-function inlining, loop unrolling for compile-time bounds, closure caching (DUPCLOSURE returns the same closure object), and immutable-upvalue capture with no allocation (~90% of upvalues are not mutated). Compiler throughput ~950K lines/sec/core. String hashing is an ARX/lookup3-style hash (LuaJIT 2.1-inspired) replicated in BytecodeBuilder so compile-time and runtime hashes match (lstring.cpp:10-16).

Luau pairs()/next() iterate array part then hash part in NODE-SLOT order, which depends on hash values and rehash history — NOT insertion order. This conflicts with grabby-aliens' insertion-ordered-map requirement. Lua/Luau spec leaves order unspecified, so diverging (insertion-ordered) keeps compat while satisfying determinism, but is a deliberate departure from Luau's table internals.

Core f64 arithmetic in the VM is plain IEEE-754 (no x87, no implicit FMA contraction), so add/sub/mul/div/sqrt are bit-identical native-vs-wasm32 (wasm mandates IEEE-754). The non-deterministic surface is transcendental/libm functions (sin, cos, exp, pow, fmod) which Luau routes to the platform libm — bit-results differ across OS/arch/wasm. A from-scratch rustia must supply its own deterministic math (e.g. the pure-Rust `libm` crate) to keep cross-platform bit-exactness.

implications_for_rustia: ADOPT register VM + 32-bit fixed-width instruction encoding with A/B/C register bytes and an AUX word — it is fully portable to Rust and wasm32 and is the single highest-ROI structural decision; it cuts dispatched-instruction count vs a stack VM.

Computed-goto dispatch DOES NOT port: safe Rust has no goto, and even C computed-goto degrades on wasm32 (wasm has no indirect-branch-to-label; LLVM lowers address-of-label to a br_table switch, collapsing per-opcode BTB specialization). On native, the closest Rust equivalent is a function-pointer threaded interpreter using guaranteed tail calls (`become`, currently unstable explicit_tail_calls) or a loop+match the compiler turns into a jump table; on wasm the winning move is emitting the WASM tail-call extension (return_call), which modern engines support — but Rust will not emit it from plain code, so this needs a custom dispatch shim. Treat dispatch as a per-target strategy, not one design.

On wasm32, INVERT Luau's value decision: 32-bit pointers make NaN-boxing attractive — an 8-byte NaN-boxed value can carry a double or a 32-bit GC handle + tag, halving value memory (16B->8B) and roughly doubling value cache density. The cost is the native 3xf32 vector no longer fits inline and must be boxed/handled separately. This is a genuine fork: 16-byte tagged-union (Luau-faithful, simplest) vs 8-byte NaN-box (wasm-memory-optimal). NaN-boxing requires NaN canonicalization for determinism.

The int64 integer subtype Luau added in release 727 (LUA_TINTEGER) is the cleanest resolution of grabby's f64-determinism tension: rustia can ship a first-class deterministic integer carrier AND Q16.16 helpers while staying Luau-compatible, instead of forcing a float-free host boundary. Worth adopting early since it touches value layout, arithmetic opcodes, and the serde bridge.

REPLICATE the self-patching inline cache (cached node slot in the instruction's C byte, keyed on interned-string pointer/id identity) — it is determinism-safe (affects only speed, never observed values) provided bytecode lives in mutable memory (a Vec<u32> is fine) and strings are interned with stable identity. This plus interned-key tables substitutes for a full hidden-class system for the common fixed-field-name access pattern.

REPLICATE load-time import resolution and the FASTCALL builtin path: these are where Luau approaches native speed on real code. In Rust, builtins as `fn(&mut VM, regs) -> i32` in a static table, invoked without a script call frame, map cleanly. The safeenv guard concept (skip the optimization if globals were mutated) is needed for correctness.

GC: an incremental, NON-moving, NON-generational mark&sweep with allocation-driven (fuel-compatible, NOT wall-clock) pacing is the determinism-friendly target and matches the steppable-VM requirement directly — drive GC steps off the same deterministic fuel counter. Non-moving keeps pointers/handles stable for inline caches. For Send+Sync N-independent-VMs, give each VM its own single-threaded heap (no cross-VM sharing); a hand-rolled mark&sweep or `gc-arena` (non-moving, brand-lifetime) are the realistic Rust options.

Tables MUST diverge from Luau on iteration order: use insertion-ordered maps (grabby hard constraint). Keep Luau's array+hash hybrid for performance but make next()/pairs() insertion-ordered. This stays within Lua's 'unspecified order' contract, so Luau-script compat is preserved.

Native runtime codegen is moot in-browser, so for the wasm32 target the interpreter IS the product: dispatch quality, value size (NaN-box), and builtin/FASTCALL coverage decide whether rustia beats koto. Reserve any native JIT effort for the native target only, and recognize its realistic ceiling (~2x over a good interpreter for a method-JIT) — do not over-invest there relative to interpreter tuning.

Determinism requires rustia to NOT use platform libm: ship a pure-Rust deterministic math library (e.g. the `libm` crate, or a fixed-point math layer) for sin/cos/exp/pow/fmod so results are bit-identical native-vs-wasm. Core +,-,*,/ ,sqrt on f64 are already bit-deterministic and need no special handling.

result.summary: The single most decisive prior art for rustia is Deegen / LuaJIT Remake (sillycross, Stanford; OOPSLA'21 copy-and-patch + arXiv 2411.11469): an automatically-generated VM where (a) the INTERPRETER uses CPS tail-call/context-threaded dispatch and is already ~31% faster than LuaJIT's hand-written asm interpreter and ~179% faster than PUC Lua, and (b) a baseline JIT built with copy-and-patch generates code at 1.62 GB/s with sub-ms latency, landing within ~34% of LuaJIT (full optimizing). This is the SOTA target. CRITICAL WASM CAVEAT: the two flagship native techniques DO NOT transfer to a wasm32 host. Copy-and-patch needs to memcpy+patch native machine bytes (impossible in wasm's Harvard/immutable-code model), and tail-call dispatch — the fastest native dispatch — is measured 1.2x (Firefox) to 4.6x (wasmtime) SLOWER than a plain switch loop when itself compiled to wasm. So rustia needs a split: a portable register-bytecode interpreter with a big br_table/switch dispatch loop for the wasm path, optionally tiered up by copy-and-patch (or cranelift) baseline JIT ONLY on native targets. Determinism is achievable for f64 on the 5 IEEE-754 basic ops (+,-,*,/,sqrt) bit-identically across x86/ARM/wasm IF FMA contraction is disabled and no transcendentals from a platform libm are used; the proven recipe (rapier physics) is pure-Rust libm. Fixed-point (Q16.16/i64) remains the only zero-risk guarantee and dovetails with the float-free boundary already in grabby.

key_findings.finding: The fastest known Lua interpreter (LJR, arXiv 2411.11469) is built by generating, per-bytecode, C++ handler functions that end in [[clang::musttail]] continuation calls (CPS / 'context threading'). This compiles each opcode to its own machine-code fragment and turns dispatch into fallthrough/tail-jumps rather than one central indirect branch — already ~31% faster than LuaJIT's hand-written assembly interpreter and ~179% faster than PUC-Lua across 44 benchmarks. Rust now has the same capability via nightly `become` + `extern "rust-preserve-none"`.

key_findings.topic: Tail-call dispatch is a TRAP on wasm
key_findings.finding: mattkeeter (2026-04) measured the identical tail-call (become/preserve-none) VM that is 1.6x FASTER than a plain Rust match-loop VM on ARM64 native to be 1.2x slower (Firefox), 3.7x slower (Chrome), and 4.6x slower (wasmtime) once compiled to wasm. Reason: wasm has no computed goto / no addressable code; tail-call dispatch becomes return_call/call_indirect through a function table, which defeats the host engine's own register allocation and inlining. The opposite of native.

key_findings.topic: Best dispatch when the engine itself is wasm
key_findings.finding: On a wasm32 host the winner is a single large switch/loop lowered to br_table (one bounds-checked jump table), NOT threading. Computed goto does not exist in wasm by construction (Harvard architecture, code not addressable, structured control flow only). The wasm tail-call proposal (return_call/return_call_indirect, shipped in V8/wasm 3.0) helps proper-tail-call languages with stack growth, not interpreter dispatch speed. Native-clang experiments show tail-calls only ~10-12% over switch even where they help; on wasm they regress.

Stencils are pre-compiled (at build time, by LLVM) native object-code fragments with relocation 'holes'; runtime codegen is just memcpy + scalar adds, no LLVM at runtime. LJR's baseline JIT emits 1.62 GB/s of machine code, ~91 bytes per Lua bytecode, compiled all 44 benchmarks (17,197 bytecodes) in <1 ms, and runs ~34% slower than full LuaJIT / 4.6x faster than PUC-Lua. This is GREAT for native tiering but fundamentally requires writing executable native bytes — impossible inside wasm32-unknown-unknown.

key_findings.topic: Copy-and-patch DOES have a wasm-stencil variant
key_findings.finding: The same group's WasmNow compiles wasm 4.9x-6.5x faster than Chrome's Liftoff baseline and produces 39%-63% faster code using 1666 stencils / 35 kB. BUT this is a wasm engine running on NATIVE (it emits native code from wasm input). It is not a way to JIT from inside a wasm sandbox. It is relevant only if rustia ever ships a native engine, not for the in-browser path.

key_findings.topic: Runtime wasm-emitting JIT from inside wasm (Wingo)
key_findings.finding: Andy Wingo (wingolog 2022-08) showed you CAN generate a new wasm module at runtime that imports the main module's memory + indirect function table, instantiate it, and patch new funcrefs into the table for call_indirect dispatch. Feasible but: WebAssembly.instantiate of a fresh module per hot function is heavyweight, sync-compile is size-capped in browsers (sync compile limited to ~4KB on main thread in some engines; large modules must be async), and the call_indirect adds indirection. Wingo's own conclusion: prefer 'offline JIT' (Wizer snapshot / AOT) over runtime emission. Verdict: not worth it for per-agent AI hotpaths.

key_findings.topic: AOT: compile Luau script -> wasm module
key_findings.finding: Technically strongest in-browser speedup path (run scripts at near-native via the host's optimizing tier), but breaks several hard constraints: (1) requires a wasm assembler + a per-script instantiate step; (2) loses the steppable-fuel/recursion VM (host wasm has no deterministic fuel unless you inject gas counters, which wasmtime supports but browsers do not); (3) GC/dynamic-typing semantics of Luau need a runtime anyway. Best used only for fully-typed hot kernels, not general scripts.

Luau deliberately does NOT NaN-box; it uses a 16-byte tagged value (8-byte double/pointer payload + tag) because it makes native 3-wide SIMD vectors a first-class type and keeps the C/Rust code branch-predictable. NaN-boxing (8 bytes) saves memory (priority #2) but costs mask/shift on every access and conflicts with storing a real f64 vector type. Tradeoff is live for rustia given low-memory priority.

key_findings.topic: Luau table / call optimizations to copy
key_findings.finding: Inline caching of field hash-slot (compiler predicts slot, VM corrects) blended with LuaJIT HREFs; GETIMPORT resolves global chains (math.max) at load time with deopt on getfenv/setfenv/loadstring; FASTCALL dispatches builtins (math.*, bit32.*, type, rawget) inline without a stack frame (~'slightly slower than core instructions'); specialized bytecode for ipairs/pairs/next; branch-free binary-search + cached #t; table templates for literals. Compiler does inlining + loop unrolling + constant folding at -O2; bytecode interpreter is ~16KB on x64 (fits I-cache).

key_findings.topic: Inline caches / hidden classes for Rust tables
key_findings.finding: V8/JSC-style hidden classes (shapes/maps) give monomorphic field access in O(1) with a shape-id guard. For a Send+Sync deterministic VM the shape table must be per-VM or behind Arc; insertion-ordered map requirement (determinism) is compatible with shape transitions if shapes record insertion order. LJR shows generic IC API auto-generated for property access, +4% typical / +10% on IC-heavy code via inline-slab + self-modifying patchable jumps — but SMC is native-only; on wasm an IC degrades to a guarded branch + side table.

key_findings.topic: Deterministic f64 across native+wasm is achievable but narrow
key_findings.finding: WebAssembly guarantees: if neither inputs nor output of an fp op is NaN, the result of +,-,*,/,sqrt,min,max,nearest etc is bit-identical across ALL platforms (round-to-nearest-even, no extended precision, no x87). The two killers are (1) FMA contraction (a*b+c fused to one rounding) — wasm has NO scalar fma except relaxed-simd; Rust/LLVM does NOT contract by default unless mul_add or fast-math is used, so just never call f64::mul_add; (2) transcendentals (sin/cos/exp/pow/log) which differ per platform libm. Fix: use the pure-Rust `libm` crate (the rapier physics engine ships cross-platform determinism this way) for ALL math, never the system/std intrinsics.

key_findings.topic: Luau is f64-only — the core tension
key_findings.finding: Luau has no integer subtype; all numbers are f64. Grabby's float-free boundary + Q16.16 fixed-point means rustia must either (a) keep f64 internally but enforce the libm + no-FMA discipline to get bit-identical f64 (then expose only int/Q16.16 at the host boundary), or (b) represent Luau 'number' as fixed-point/integer where the sim needs determinism and accept Luau-semantics divergence. Option (a) is more Luau-compatible (priority #4); option (b) is zero-risk determinism (priority #1) but non-conformant.

v128 maps to native SSE2/NEON and is phase-5 shipped. Useful for: 16-byte tagged-value moves, vector3 math (Luau's native vector type), batch GC mark scanning, and string compare/hash. NaN-boxing+SIMD synergy is weak (NaN-box is scalar). SIMD won't speed up the dispatch loop itself. Determinism note: core wasm SIMD fp is deterministic under the same non-NaN rule; AVOID relaxed-SIMD (fma, approximate ops) which is explicitly non-deterministic.

Register bytecode (Lua 5/Luau/LuaJIT style) already beats stack bytecode by eliminating push/pop traffic (~30-50% fewer dispatches typical in literature). Superinstruction fusion (e.g. ADD+MOV, GETFIELD+CALL→NAMECALL, loop-test+jump) cuts dispatch count further; Luau's FORGLOOP/NAMECALL/FASTCALL are exactly fused superinstructions. On a wasm host where each dispatch is a relatively expensive br_table, REDUCING dispatch count via fat register superinstructions is the single highest-leverage wasm-portable win.

implications_for_rustia: Dispatch strategy MUST be target-split, not universal. On native: CPS tail-call / context-threaded (Rust nightly `become` + rust-preserve-none) is the proven fastest and is what beats LuaJIT's interpreter. On wasm32: that SAME technique regresses up to 4.6x — use a single big match -> br_table loop instead. Design the interpreter so the opcode handlers are written once but the DISPATCH glue is cfg(target_arch="wasm32")-conditional (switch-loop) vs native (tail-call chain). This is the highest-impact architectural decision in this stream.

Copy-and-patch JIT belongs on the NATIVE tier only. Plan a two-tier engine: (tier 0) portable register-bytecode interpreter everywhere; (tier 1) copy-and-patch OR cranelift baseline JIT compiled in under #[cfg(not(target_arch="wasm32"))]. In-browser, rustia stays interpreter-only — accept that and make the interpreter excellent. Do NOT attempt runtime wasm-module emission for hot functions (Wingo path): instantiate cost + sync-compile size caps + call_indirect indirection make it lose to a good interpreter for short per-agent AI scripts.

Minimize dispatch COUNT for the wasm path: a register VM + aggressive superinstruction fusion (Luau's FORGLOOP/NAMECALL/FASTCALL/GETIMPORT) is the most wasm-portable speedup because each br_table dispatch is comparatively expensive in wasm. Spend optimization budget on fat fused opcodes and inline caches that degrade gracefully to a guarded branch + side table on wasm (no self-modifying code available).

Determinism is solvable for f64 WITHOUT abandoning Luau number semantics: enforce (1) the pure-Rust `libm` crate for every transcendental (the rapier-proven recipe), (2) never emit f64::mul_add / never enable fast-math / avoid relaxed-SIMD, (3) restrict to the bit-identical IEEE-754 op set. This keeps full Luau f64 compat (priority #4) while preserving bit-for-bit native+wasm (priority #1). Fixed-point/Q16.16 stays the zero-risk fallback and matches grabby's existing float-free host boundary — recommend f64-internal-with-libm-discipline as default, fixed-point as a build-mode escape hatch.

Value layout is a real fork: Luau's 16-byte tagged value is faster/branch-friendlier and enables a native vector3 type (good for game AI), but NaN-boxing (8 bytes) directly serves priority #2 (low memory) and wasm cache pressure. Given priorities (speed #1, memory #2), prototype BOTH and benchmark; NaN-boxing's mask/shift may be cheaper than 2x memory traffic on wasm's linear memory. This should be one of the 5 explored directions.

Inline caches + hidden-classes/shapes must be designed Send+Sync and insertion-order-preserving from day one (determinism + 'N VMs on a thread pool'). Shapes can record insertion order so IC + ordered-map are compatible. On native an IC can use patchable SMC (LJR-style, +4-10%); on wasm it must be a guarded branch into a side table — design the IC abstraction to compile to both.
candidate_directions: Deegen-inspired dual-dispatch interpreter: single opcode-handler source, CPS tail-call dispatch on native (target LuaJIT-interpreter-class speed, ~31% over LuaJIT), big br_table switch-loop on wasm — the recommended baseline architecture.

Native-only tiering: tier-0 portable interpreter + tier-1 copy-and-patch baseline JIT (1.6 GB/s codegen, within ~34% of LuaJIT) gated behind cfg(not(wasm32)); wasm stays interpreter-only. Alternative tier-1: cranelift for maintainability vs copy-and-patch for compile speed.

Register VM with maximal superinstruction fusion + Luau-style FASTCALL/GETIMPORT/NAMECALL, optimizing the wasm path by minimizing dispatch count rather than dispatch cost — the most portable single-codebase win.
Value-representation fork to benchmark: 16-byte Luau tagged value (SIMD vector type, branch-friendly) vs 8-byte NaN-boxed (low memory, less wasm linear-memory traffic).

Determinism mode fork: (a) f64-internal with mandatory pure-Rust libm + no-FMA discipline for full Luau compat with bit-identical results, vs (b) fixed-point/Q16.16 number representation for zero-risk determinism matching grabby's float-free boundary, selectable at build time.
AOT script->wasm for fully-typed hot kernels only (not general scripts), accepting loss of deterministic fuel/stepping for those kernels — niche, low priority.
open_questions: Does Rust's nightly `become`/rust-preserve-none stabilize on a timeline rustia can depend on, and does it work under wasm32 codegen at all (or must the wasm path always be the switch-loop)? Need to test musttail emission on wasm32 target.

Can a copy-and-patch baseline JIT be built in Rust without LLVM-at-build-time stencil generation tooling (Deegen relies on clang asm-goto/CallBr + LLVM build-time)? What is the Rust-native stencil pipeline (dynasm? inkwell at build time? hand-written .o stencils)?
Exact magnitude of the br_table dispatch penalty on wasm vs the native tail-call path for OUR opcode set — needs a microbenchmark before committing the dual-dispatch design.

For deterministic f64: is the pure-Rust `libm` crate bit-identical between native x86-64 and wasm32 for the full transcendental set we need, across all rounding edge cases, and is it fast enough vs system libm (it is typically slower)?
If we keep Luau f64 semantics, how do we reconcile with the host's Q16.16 boundary — do scripts compute in f64 and quantize at the boundary, and is that quantization itself deterministic?
Does insertion-ordered table + hidden-class shape transitions interact correctly when keys are deleted/re-added (shape explosion / determinism of shape ids across VMs)?

Steppable deterministic fuel: counting bytecodes is easy in the interpreter; how is fuel preserved if/when a function tiers up to the native copy-and-patch JIT (must inject fuel decrements into generated stencils)?

result.summary: grabby-aliens uses koto 0.16.1 in three places: (1) view console REPL (view/src/console.rs, feature "arc"), (2) scenario procedural generation (scenario/src/lib.rs, features "arc"+"serde"), and (3) a throwaway perf bake-off (ai_bakeoff/, feature "arc"). The exact koto API surface consumed is small and stable: Koto::with_settings/default, prelude().add_fn/insert, exports().get, compile_and_run(CompileArgs::...export_top_level_ids), call_function(KValue,&[KValue]), value_to_string, and KValue/KNumber(I64|F64) pattern-matching in host fns. The determinism contract is the dominant constraint: bit-identical across native + wasm32 + x86_64-linux + aarch64-mac, enforced by FNV-1a golden hashes pinned to single cross-arch constants, a strict float-free host<->script boundary (only i64/Q16.16; all f64 in Rust), insertion-ordered maps, FNV-1a-seeded ChaCha8 substreams, integer epsilon-greedy, and a DETERMINISTIC instruction-fuel limit that must REPLACE koto's wall-clock Instant-based ExecutionTimeout. Perf bar: koto measured ~5.4 us/decision (~39x the 0.14 us Rust-native floor); rustia must beat koto and ideally approach native, which would let the per-tick-per-agent AI hot path move back into script. The serde requirement is koto::serde::from_koto_value -> a serde-derive ScenarioSpec with deny_unknown_fields/default, same validate() path as serde_yaml.

key_findings.topic: Koto embedding API surface actually used (the binding contract rustia must mirror)
key_findings.finding: Exact methods consumed across the repo: `Koto::default()`, `Koto::with_settings(KotoSettings::default().with_execution_limit(Duration))`, `koto.prelude() -> &KMap` then `.add_fn(name, move |ctx| -> Result<KValue>)` and `.insert(name, KValue)`, `koto.exports() -> &KMap` then `.get(name) -> Option<KValue>`, `koto.compile_and_run(impl Into<CompileArgs>)`, `koto.call_function(KValue, &[KValue]) -> Result<KValue>`, `koto.value_to_string(KValue) -> Result<String>`. REPL persistence uses `CompileArgs::new(s).export_top_level_ids(true)`. Imports used: `koto::prelude::*`, `koto::runtime::{KNumber, runtime_error, CallContext, KValue}`, `koto::{CompileArgs, Koto, KotoSettings}`, `koto::serde::from_koto_value`.

Host fns receive `ctx.args() -> &[KValue]` and pattern-match `[KValue::Number(a), KValue::Number(b)]`, converting with `let a: i64 = a.into()` or `f64::from(*n)`. Numbers are `KNumber::I64(i64)` | `KNumber::F64(f64)` ONLY — no integer subtype distinct from f64 semantics beyond the I64 tag. Return values are `KValue::Number(KNumber::I64(x))`, `KValue::Str`, `KValue::Null`. Errors via `runtime_error!("...")`. `KValue::is_callable()` used to decide bare-ident call vs eval.

key_findings.topic: Koto arithmetic limitation forcing host helpers (the float-free wart)
key_findings.finding: Source-verified in ai_bakeoff/tests/koto_probe.rs: `+ - * %` between two I64 stay I64 (wrapping); but `/` ALWAYS promotes to f64 even for I64/I64; there are NO `>>`, `//`, or bitwise operators; `**` is not an operator (power is a method). Therefore a float-free Q16.16 path CANNOT divide or shift in pure script — it must call host helpers `fxmul(a,b)=(a*b)>>16` and `curve(kind,x)` (LUT lookup) implemented in Rust. This is the single biggest ergonomic wart and a direct design target for rustia.

koto used with `default-features=false, features=["arc"]` so `KValue: Send+Sync` (asserted by a compile test `assert_send_sync::<KValue>()`). Model is N independent VMs across a thread pool (NOT one shared VM); ~5-10% per-borrow tax cited. NOTE the console's `KotoRepl` is stored as Bevy `NonSend` because that VM instance is !Send in practice (single-threaded REPL); the arc feature is what makes the multi-VM sim path viable.

scenario/src/lib.rs::from_koto_seeded does `koto::serde::from_koto_value(koto.exports().clone()) -> ScenarioSpec` (koto feature "serde", serde derive). The script `export`s a map with the SAME shape as the YAML. ScenarioSpec uses `#[derive(Serialize,Deserialize)]`, `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` (a typo'd key ERRORS), `#[serde(default)]` and `#[serde(default="fn")]`. The SAME `spec.validate()?.resolve()` runs for both YAML (serde_yaml 0.9) and Koto — format is decoupled from the data model. rustia must provide an equivalent `from_value::<T: Deserialize>` deserializer.

key_findings.topic: Koto's execution limit is non-deterministic by construction
key_findings.finding: koto_runtime-0.16.1/src/vm.rs: `ExecutionTimeout` uses `instant::Instant` (wall-clock) with an ADAPTIVE instruction interval (`interval_instructions` recomputed from elapsed seconds each check). It counts `instructions_since_last_check` but the deadline test is time-based. The plan explicitly forbids this for sim-side scripts and requires a monotonic INSTRUCTION-COUNT fuel budget dropped in at the same `execute_instructions` check site (vm.rs:674-697). rustia must ship a deterministic fuel meter as a first-class primitive, not bolt on a wall-clock timer.

vm.rs execute_instructions returns on `ControlFlow::Yield(value)` setting `ExecutionState::Suspended`, with a `continue_running -> ReturnOrYield{Return|Yield}` API. This maps onto the intended scripted-agent model: a coroutine yielding a `ControlInput` per tick (design §3). rustia needs the same steppable/yield-resumable VM so deterministic fuel + recursion limits + per-tick yielding all work.

koto's KMap is backed by `indexmap` (koto_runtime Cargo.toml dep) -> insertion-ordered iteration, which the plan calls determinism-friendly. Note the SIM side uses BTreeMap/sorted iteration instead; the contract is: any map whose iteration order affects sim state must be deterministically ordered (insertion or sorted). rustia must guarantee insertion-ordered map iteration.

key_findings.topic: The determinism golden methodology (what must be bit-identical)
key_findings.finding: FNV-1a (offset 0xcbf29ce484222325, prime 0x100000001b3) folds state into a u64 hash, pinned to a SINGLE shared cross-arch constant (deliberately NOT per-platform, so a one-OS red is a real finding). f64 folded via `to_bits` with -0.0->+0.0 canonicalization; records SimId-sorted. sim/tests/determinism_golden.rs pins physics=9715618621526538300, CCD=1828383301069731689, economy=16747376415410472512. ai_bakeoff pins AI state_hash=0x31c6ec2734ea6fa2 and CRUCIALLY the koto-int path reproduces it EXACTLY (koto_equiv.rs) -> float-free Koto is determinism-equivalent to native.

All transcendentals go through `libm` (NEVER std sin/cos/powf — a real cross-libc crack the audit found). f64 is permitted ONLY for one-time LUT construction (built via libm so bit-identical cross-arch), never in the hot path. Q16.16 LUT lookups use integer index + integer linear interpolation (`a + fx_mul(b-a, frac)`); LUT index rounding is itself called out as a desync class. rustia's any-float surface must route through libm and be pinned by a golden.

Seeded `rand_chacha::ChaCha8Rng` (portable; NOT StdRng/thread_rng). Per-entity substreams `seed = FNV-1a(entity_id, tick)` so randomness is DECOUPLED from iteration order (proven count-independent in determinism.rs). The seed hash MUST be a fixed portable algorithm (FNV-1a or hardcoded-key SipHash), NEVER std::DefaultHasher (per-process randomized). Exploration is INTEGER epsilon-greedy: `(rng.next_u32() & 1023) < 51` (~0.05), never a float compare. Scenario gen uses a host-side SplitMix64 (Rust integer math) exposed to script as rand()/rand_range() so generation reproduces regardless of script float impl.

key_findings.topic: Performance bar and the exact bake-off workload
key_findings.finding: Native floor 0.14 us/decision; koto-int 5.4 us (~39x); koto-float (no host calls) 4.0 us (~29x) — so ~74% of cost is the interpreter VM itself, not the float-free boundary (a fork for integer ops would NOT rescue hot-path perf). Bar: AI must fit <=5 ms of a 20 ms (50 Hz) tick single-threaded on the SLOWEST target. Native does 10k agents in 1.43 ms; koto-int blows 5 ms above ~900 agents, koto-float ~1250. Workload = IAUS product-of-considerations (4 considerations x 6 actions) + 1.25x momentum to last action + integer epsilon-greedy + SARSA(lambda) replacing trace (ALPHA=0.1, GAMMA_LAMBDA=0.9) + social contagion (k=0.05, 4 neighbors); all Q16.16.

key_findings.finding: Criterion 0.5, harness=false, profile.release opt-level=3. Sweep n in {1000,2000,5000,10000} single-threaded; koto benched at {1000,5000} with sample_size(20). `b.iter(|| { world.tick_with(sel); black_box(world.state_hash()) })`. Throughput::Elements(n). MUST build `wasm32-unknown-unknown` (proven via `cargo build --release --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`). koto uses the `instant` crate for wasm-compatible Instant. JIT is moot in browser (wasmtime can't JIT on web; Bevy single-threaded on web). Web is single-threaded twice over (no wasm threads + single-threaded Bevy scheduler). The plan warns the wasm interpreter tax could be ~4x (bytecode-VM-inside-bytecode-VM with GC pressure) and that a MEASURED browser number is still an open gate, not extrapolated.

Hot-reload = re-eval with NO compile step (koto's instant re-eval is a cited win); measure save->re-eval->visible-change latency. Compile/iteration time matters. IDE/LSP expected (koto ships an LSP). Embedding API judged 'clean'; the missing integer ops are 'a real ergonomic wart for sim math'. Console REPL DX: functions-ARE-commands (bare `quit`, `spawn 100 80`, `e = spawn 10 10`), persistent top-level bindings via export_top_level_ids, value_to_string for display, a clean channel/effect-queue host model (NO UnsafeWorldCell).

key_findings.topic: Host-bridge architecture pattern rustia must support cleanly
key_findings.finding: Console host fns never borrow the World: they push `ConsoleEffect` enum variants onto an `Arc<Mutex<Vec<Effect>>>` (WRITE side) applied later by the system that owns World access, and READ a refreshed `Arc<Mutex<WorldView>>` snapshot. This 'channel + scheduled message-bus' model (vs the old slowchop_koto UnsafeWorldCell transmute) is the determinism+parallelism-safe reference design. Host closures must be `move` and (under arc) Send+Sync-compatible (scenario gen uses Arc<AtomicU64> just to satisfy the Send+Sync bound on native fns).

implications_for_rustia: rustia MUST provide native integer/fixed-point arithmetic that does NOT promote to f64 (integer `/`, `>>`, `//`, bitwise, integer `**`). Koto's lack of these is the documented ergonomic wart that forces host fxmul/curve helpers. First-class Q16.16 or wrapping-integer ops would remove the host-call boundary entirely for sim math.

The hot-path cost is the interpreter VM itself (koto-float still 4.0us with zero host calls). To beat the perf bar rustia needs JIT/AOT or a far faster dispatch (register VM + inline caches + computed-goto/threaded dispatch) — a fork of an interpreter for integer ops will NOT close the ~29x gap.

Deterministic instruction-fuel is a CORE primitive, not an add-on: replace koto's Instant-based adaptive ExecutionTimeout with a monotonic per-call instruction budget checked in the dispatch loop, plus a recursion-depth cap at the frame-push site. This must be bit-deterministic across native and wasm.
The VM must be steppable/yield-resumable (coroutine model): a scripted agent yields a ControlInput per tick. rustia needs ExecutionState::Suspended + continue_running equivalents from day one.

Provide a serde Deserializer (`from_value::<T>`) compatible with serde-derive structs using deny_unknown_fields + default + default=fn, so the existing ScenarioSpec deserialize path ports unchanged. Also a Serializer for round-trip parity.

Values must be Send+Sync (the arc model) to support N-VMs-across-a-threadpool; aim to make this the default, not a feature flag with a per-borrow tax. The embedding API must let host closures be plain `move` Fn + Send + Sync.
Maps MUST iterate in insertion order (indexmap-equivalent) AND rustia must make it trivial to get sorted/deterministic iteration where order feeds sim state.

All float operations rustia exposes must route through a portable transcendental impl (libm-equivalent) and be coverable by a pinned single-constant cross-arch golden; ideally rustia supports a 'float-free/deterministic mode' that capability-gates every f64-touching op (float<->string, fmod/%, float compare/sort, map-key hashing, **, int<->float coercion) out of the prelude.

The host-bridge API should make the channel/effect-queue + read-snapshot pattern natural (no unsafe World aliasing); host fns get a typed arg slice and return a Value or a runtime error, mirroring add_fn(name, |ctx| ...).

wasm32-unknown-unknown must be a tier-1 target with a wasm-compatible time source (or, better, NO reliance on wall-clock since fuel is instruction-based). A real in-browser perf number is a required gate.
Embedding ergonomics for a REPL (functions-are-commands, persistent top-level bindings, value-to-string display) and an LSP are explicit DX deciding factors — rustia should plan tooling early.

Snapshot capture/restore must be able to serialize and EXACTLY restore VM/script-visible state for MP rollback/reconcile; if scripts hold per-agent state in the hot path, that state must be in the deterministic snapshot or the checksum proves nothing.
candidate_directions: JIT/AOT-compiled rustia (native) with an instruction-fuel-metered interpreter fallback for wasm — directly targets the ~29x VM-dispatch gap that a bytecode interpreter cannot close.

Register-based bytecode VM with native i64/Q16.16 fast paths and NO f64 promotion on `/`/`>>`, plus inline caches — keeps the koto embedding ergonomics but removes the host-helper boundary and a chunk of dispatch cost.

Batched/vectorized host-entry API: 'decide N agents in one VM call' to amortize per-call marshalling (the call_function + KValue clone per agent is real overhead) — lets a slower-per-call VM still hit the aggregate budget.

A deterministic-by-construction execution mode (float-free prelude + instruction fuel + recursion cap + insertion-ordered maps + portable transcendentals) as a first-class VM configuration, so sim-side scripts are safe without per-project discipline.

Keep the grabby split (Rust-native hot path, script for cooler/infrequent leaves) but make rustia fast enough that the leaf cadence can rise from a few Hz toward per-tick — measure the crossover and expose a fuel/LOD knob.
open_questions: What is rustia's measured per-decision cost on wasm32 in a real browser (the gate koto never cleared)? The native win is moot if the in-browser tax is ~4x.

Can rustia's deterministic-mode produce bit-identical results to the SAME pinned golden constants (0x31c6ec2734ea6fa2 for AI; the libm-LUT path) across x86_64-linux + aarch64-mac + wasm32 — i.e. is a Luau-derived numeric stack as cross-arch-stable as the libm/Q16.16 discipline requires?

Luau numbers are f64-only with no integer subtype — how does rustia reconcile full Luau compat with the float-free i64/Q16.16 sim boundary? (Provide integer intrinsics? A fixed-point library? A deterministic f64 mode pinned by golden?) This is the central tension the plan flags.
If rustia is ~10x koto, does the per-tick-per-agent scripted hot path actually move back into script, and what batched/coroutine API makes that pay off without per-call marshalling killing it?
What is the memory footprint per VM / per agent? Priority #2 is low memory but no hard byte budget is stated in grabby; per-agent Q-tables/traces already flagged as a snapshot/bandwidth concern.
Can rustia snapshot+restore full script-visible per-agent state for MP rollback (predict/reconcile) cheaply enough to capture every SNAPSHOT_EVERY, or does it need delta/coarse-cadence capture?
Does rustia need an LSP and what is its hot-reload (save->re-eval->visible) latency vs koto's instant re-eval — the DX deciding axis gak cares most about?
